articles.title: Faceless YouTube with AI: A Realistic Beginner's Guide to Planning, Scripting and Publishing Your First Videos
articles.excerpt: Start a faceless YouTube channel with AI help — no hype. How to pick a topic, write a script, record a voiceover, and meet YouTube's rules.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Faceless YouTube with AI: A Realistic Beginner's Guide to Planning, Scripting and Publishing Your First Videos
AI Tools & Online Business

Faceless YouTube with AI: A Realistic Beginner's Guide to Planning, Scripting and Publishing Your First Videos

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · youtube, ai-tools

Picture this: you have ten useful videos in mind, a phone, and a quiet corner of a room — but no desire to be on camera. That is enough to start a faceless YouTube channel, one where the creator never appears on screen and the video is carried by a voiceover, on-screen text, animation, screen recordings, photographs, or stock footage. The format appeals to beginners: no camera-ready room, no on-camera performance, and recording in short sessions. AI can help with an outline, a script draft, a voiceover, captions, or a thumbnail. It does not remove the work that makes a channel worth watching: a clear idea, accurate information, a script that sounds like a person talking, and visuals that match the words. This guide is built around a simple test: ten videos, one topic, one format, one video a week. By the end you will have real evidence — watch time, comments, and your own honest answer to whether you enjoyed making them — instead of a guess. It makes no income promise. YouTube's rules matter more than any tool, so they come first.

The rules that decide whether a channel can earn

YouTube does not ban faceless channels, and it does not require you to appear on camera. It does require original, useful content, and it checks that before it pays you anything.

The YouTube Partner Program

The YouTube Partner Program (YPP) is the route to ad revenue. The thresholds below are from YouTube's own Help pages, checked 18 November 2026. They change — and a big change arrives on 1 February 2027 — so re-check YouTube Help before you plan around them.

TierWhat it unlocksWhat you need
Lower tierFan funding, Shopping, Creator Partnerships500 subscribers, 3 public uploads in the last 90 days, and either 3,000 qualified watch hours in 12 months or 3 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days
Full tierAd revenue and YouTube Premium revenue1,000 subscribers and either 4,000 qualified watch hours in 12 months or 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days

You also need to live in a country where YPP is available, have a linked AdSense account, have two-step verification on, and have no active Community Guidelines strikes. Meeting the numbers only gets you a review, which usually takes about a month.

From 1 February 2027, the bar rises for new applicants to the full tier: 1,000 subscribers plus either 8,000 qualified watch hours in 365 days or 20 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days. Channels already in YPP are not affected, and the 500-subscriber tier does not change. From the same date, Shorts ad-pool earnings need 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, and channels must stay active (for example, 1,000 watch hours in 365 days or 5 Shorts every 90 days). Existing partners must accept the updated terms in YouTube Studio by 31 January 2027.

AI disclosure: the realism test

YouTube's rule is about realism, not about whether you used AI at all. Disclose content that is realistic and was generated or meaningfully altered with AI — a real person shown saying or doing something they did not, altered footage of a real event or place, a realistic scene that never happened, or AI-generated music as the main focus. Set this when you upload in YouTube Studio: in the Attributes section, under "AI use," choose Yes or No. No disclosure is normally needed for AI help with a script, outline, title, thumbnail, or captions; for minor edits; for clearly unrealistic content; or for cloning your own voice. YouTube says disclosing alone will not limit a video's audience or eligibility to earn, and it can also label a video automatically — for content made with its own tools, files carrying Content Credentials (C2PA) metadata, or content its systems detect as AI-generated. Not disclosing when you should can lead to penalties including removal from the Partner Program.

Two policies that catch faceless channels

  • Reused content: repurposing other people's material without adding significant original commentary, substantive changes, or educational value. A stock-footage license does not settle this — YouTube asks what you added.
  • Inauthentic content: videos that look templated, or feel repetitive after watching several in a row. Renamed from "repetitious content" in July 2025, it says each video's substance should be "materially varied." A shared format is fine; a shared script with different nouns swapped in is not. This is the policy that ends most low-effort AI channels.

Start with ten videos, not a channel

Do not start with "AI" or "money" as a topic. Start with a specific question people already ask, in a subject you can research for months. "Beginners setting up a first small balcony garden" will carry ten videos; "gardening" will not. Take Rosa, a fictional beginner: she grows herbs on a rented balcony and keeps getting the same questions from friends — which herbs survive wind, how often to water basil, what to do when mint takes over. Her ten-video list writes itself: one herb per video, plus watering, soil, pots, and her first-month mistakes. Before recording anything, write down your ten ideas; if you cannot reach ten, the topic is too narrow.

Step 1: Research before you write

AI can help organize research. It cannot replace it. Find the real question: search YouTube and Google for the exact phrasing people use, read the comments on the top three videos, and note what is missing — that gap is your video. Check two independent sources, such as a manufacturer's guide and a reputable tutorial; if they disagree, say so or leave the point out. Test the steps yourself first, even roughly: you will find the step everyone skips and the mistake a beginner is most likely to make. Use an AI assistant to organize notes into an outline, then verify every factual claim — AI tools can invent plausible details, prices, and statistics.

Step 2: Write a script that sounds spoken

For a 6–8 minute video, spend the first 20 seconds stating the problem and the outcome: "Basil keeps dying on your balcony. Here is the watering mistake that kills it, and the fix that takes two minutes." Then cover three points, one idea each, with a concrete example, and end with one small action the viewer can do today. Spoken English runs roughly 130–150 words per minute, so a 6-minute video needs about 800–900 words. Read the script aloud and time it, cutting any sentence you stumble over twice.

Step 3: Choose a voice

Record your own voice if you can — a phone in a quiet room is enough, and short sections let you re-do one sentence at a time. An AI voice works if recording is genuinely difficult, but check the license first: a free plan may not include commercial use, and imitating a real person is a different matter from a generic synthetic voice. Text and music only suits visual walkthroughs, but keep text to a few words per screen.

Step 4: Build visuals that match the words

The most common beginner mistake is letting the visuals drift from the narration — the voice talks about watering while the screen shows a random garden. For each paragraph, write one line describing the visual: "Show the wet soil close-up." Use your own photographs and short clips first — even phone footage proves you did it. Use stock footage sparingly, and note each clip's license. Keep on-screen text simple, a few words at a time.

Make the thumbnail separately: one clear image, one idea, three words or fewer, readable at phone size.

Step 5: Edit for clarity, then publish the same way every time

You need clean cuts, steady pacing, and captions — not advanced effects. Cut dead air and repeated words. Keep each visual on screen only as long as the narration needs it, usually 3–8 seconds. Add captions: many viewers watch without sound. Check the audio before exporting — no sudden volume jumps, no music louder than the voice. Watch it once on a phone before uploading. Free editors such as DaVinci Resolve and CapCut's free plan are enough to start.

Publishing is a checklist, done the same way every time:

  • Title says what the video does, in the words a viewer would search for
  • Description opens with one or two summary sentences, then the main steps
  • AI-use question answered honestly in YouTube Studio
  • Audience setting chosen (made for kids or not — get this right, it matters)
  • Thumbnail checked at small size on a phone
  • Video added to a series playlist

Then commit to the run: ten videos, one topic, one format, on a schedule you can keep — for most beginners, one video a week. After ten, look at the evidence: which videos kept viewers watching, and which comments asked for a follow-up. Do not judge a channel on its first three videos.

What it costs to start

You can start for $0 — pay only when a free option is clearly slowing you down. ChatGPT Free ($0) for outlines and drafts; Plus $20/month. Your own voice costs $0; ElevenLabs Starter is $6/month ($5/month billed annually) and includes a commercial license, while its free plan (10,000 credits a month) is non-commercial use only. DaVinci Resolve is free; CapCut Pro is $19.99/month; Descript's free plan covers 60 media minutes a month and Hobbyist is $16/month billed annually ($24 month-to-month). Canva Free ($0) is enough for thumbnails; Pro is $144/year or $18/month. Prices are US list prices checked 18 November 2026, before tax — verify before paying. A realistic starter budget is $0 for the first ten videos.

Money, honestly

Income from a faceless channel is potential, never guaranteed. Most new channels earn nothing for months, and many never reach the Partner Program thresholds — especially now that the bar rises in February 2027. Ad revenue depends on topic, audience location, time of year, and watch time, none of which a beginner can predict. Affiliate links must be disclosed and sponsorships declared. Treat the first ten videos as a test, not a business plan.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Ignoring comments. Early comments are your best research — use them as your next videos.
  • Buying views or subscribers. This violates YouTube's policies and can lead to removal from the Partner Program.

Conclusion

A faceless YouTube channel with AI help is a realistic project for a beginner — not because AI does the work, but because it lowers the barrier to drafting, voiceover, captions, and editing. What still decides whether a channel works is a clear topic, accurate information, a script that sounds human, and visuals that match the words. Learn the rules before you publish, keep costs at $0 until a paid tool earns its place, and judge the channel after ten videos, not after one.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help choosing the right AI tools, planning a small content workflow, or learning to use AI for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to show my face to make money on YouTube?⌄

No. YouTube requires original content that adds value, not a face on camera. A faceless channel can join the Partner Program if it meets the thresholds and passes review.

Do I have to disclose that I used AI?⌄

Disclose realistic AI-generated or AI-altered content a viewer could mistake for real. AI help with a script, title, or thumbnail does not normally need disclosure. Answer the "AI use" question in YouTube Studio honestly.

Can I use an AI voice?⌄

Yes, if it is a generic synthetic voice or a clone of your own voice, and the license allows commercial use. ElevenLabs' free plan does not include a commercial license. Do not imitate a real person without permission.

articles.title: How to Use ChatGPT to Design Simple Ads for a Small Business
articles.excerpt: Design a simple small-business ad with ChatGPT: write a brief, draft honest copy, choose an image, build it in Canva, and test two versions.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. How to Use ChatGPT to Design Simple Ads for a Small Business
AI Tools & Online Business

How to Use ChatGPT to Design Simple Ads for a Small Business

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · chatgpt, ads

You have one afternoon, one offer, and no designer. That is enough to make a first ad — if you start with the offer instead of the tool. A small business does not need a design team: it needs one clear offer, one clear audience, and one image a person can understand in a few seconds. ChatGPT can help with the slow parts — a headline, a few lines of copy, a layout, a simple starting image — but it cannot replace your judgment, and it cannot guarantee clicks, visits, or sales.

This guide is a one-afternoon workshop: by the end you will have a brief, a headline tested on a real stranger, one finished ad file in Canva, and a plan to test it against a second version — all for $0 on free plans.

What ChatGPT can do — and what it cannot

ChatGPT is useful for drafting headlines and short descriptions, planning a layout, creating a simple starting image, and reading a draft as a first-time customer would.

It is not reliable for exact text inside an image — it often misspells words or changes a price, so add the final text in Canva instead. It does not know your colors, fonts, or logo, and it is a poor choice for real people and real products: an AI image of a cake is not your cake. For anything a buyer will judge by appearance, use a real photograph. ChatGPT can also invent a claim, so every fact must come from you. The rule: ChatGPT drafts, you decide.

The one-page brief: five answers before you open ChatGPT

Do not open ChatGPT and type "make me an ad." Start with five short answers: (1) the one offer — one product, service, or event; (2) who it is for — "parents nearby who need a birthday cake this weekend" is a brief, "everyone" is not; (3) what they should do next — visit, book, message, or click, pick one; (4) the one reason to care; (5) what must be true — the price, the dates, the location.

Here is a filled-in brief for a fictional plant shop, carried through this guide: a ready-to-gift herb set — basil, mint, and parsley — for $28, for people nearby buying a small gift for a friend who cooks. The action is to visit the shop on Saturday or message to reserve a set.

Step 1: Draft the copy in ChatGPT

Ask ChatGPT for copy — not a finished ad. Give it the brief and ask for options:

"I run a small plant shop. I am selling a ready-to-gift herb set — basil, mint, and parsley — for $28. It is for people nearby buying a small gift for a friend who cooks. The action is to visit the shop on Saturday or message us to reserve one. Please write five headlines of six words or fewer, three short descriptions of one or two sentences, and three calls to action. Use plain, friendly language. Do not add any claims I did not give you."

Ask for several options — the first headline is rarely the best — then edit the winner by hand and try the stranger test: show it to someone who does not know your business. If they cannot answer "what is it, and what do I do?" in ten seconds, the copy is not ready:

Before (ChatGPT's first draft)After (edited by hand)
"Elevate Your Culinary Journey with Our Premium Fresh Herb Collection Today!""A gift for someone who cooks. $28."
"Transform every meal with garden-fresh flavor.""Basil, mint, and parsley — ready to gift."
"Visit us today to discover the difference!""Visit Saturday, or message to reserve one."

The first version sounds like an ad. The second sounds like a shopkeeper talking to a neighbor — and it passes the stranger test.

Step 2: Make a simple image — or use a real photo

Use a real photograph when the product matters. If you sell food, plants, or handmade goods, a phone photo in good daylight, near a window on a plain surface, is usually better than an AI image.

Use a ChatGPT image when you need a simple scene or background, such as a calm illustration for a tutoring service. Describe the scene, not the ad: "Three small potted herbs — basil, mint, and parsley — in plain terracotta pots on a light wooden table, near a window, soft daylight, no text, no people, no logos." Check the result at full size for misspelled text; if it is wrong, ask for a version with no text, or use a real photo.

ChatGPT includes image generation on every plan, including Free, but the free allowance is limited and slower, and OpenAI does not publish a fixed number of images per day for any plan: Go gives you more than Free, Plus adds more complex and accurate generation, and Pro offers unlimited and faster generation, subject to abuse guardrails. The limit message inside your own ChatGPT account is the one that applies to you.

Step 3: Put the ad together in Canva

ChatGPT is a drafting tool. Canva is where the ad becomes a finished file, and its free plan is enough: start from a blank canvas in the right size, add your image, add your headline and description as real text, and add your logo. A reliable layout: the image at the top, about two-thirds of the space; the headline underneath; one or two sentences explaining the offer; and the price and the action at the bottom. Keep the text short, reuse the same colors and fonts from your Canva brand kit, and make the ad in the size for where it will appear — check the platform's own ad guide before you upload, because sizes change:

Where it will appearRecommended size
Facebook or Instagram feed1080 × 1080 px (1:1) or 1080 × 1350 px (4:5)
Facebook or Instagram Stories and Reels1080 × 1920 px (9:16)
Facebook link preview / right column1200 × 628 px (1.91:1)
Pinterest standard Pin or ad1000 × 1500 px (2:3)

Step 4: Check the ad before anyone else sees it

Check the finished file, not your memory of it. Read every word, including the price — read the price backwards, digit by digit. Is the price right? Are the dates right? Does the image show what you actually sell? Is it clear what to do next, and is the link correct? Click it yourself, remove any word you cannot prove, and look at the ad on a phone before you pay.

One label to expect: Meta applies an "AI info" label to ads it detects were created or significantly edited with generative AI — including third-party tools, detected through industry signals such as C2PA metadata — shown in the ad's "About this ad" panel, more visibly for a photorealistic AI-generated person. Minor edits such as cropping do not trigger it. For ads about social issues, elections, or politics, the advertiser must disclose AI use themselves. This is a summary of Meta's published rules as of June 2026, not legal advice.

Step 5: Test two versions, then decide with evidence

Do not spend your whole budget on one ad. Make two versions that differ in one thing only — the same image with two different headlines, or the same headline with two different images. For our plant shop, version A could use "A gift for someone who cooks. $28." and version B "Basil, mint, and parsley — ready to gift." Run both briefly on a small budget and compare them on the same measure: clicks, or completions of the action you asked for. Change one thing at a time, give it enough time — a few hours is not a test — then keep the winner and test again. Keep expectations honest: a good ad usually brings a few inquiries or orders, not a transformation. If an ad does not work, the offer, audience, or message needs to change — not the tool.

What it costs

You can make your first ad for $0 on free plans. ChatGPT and Canva do not include ad spend, which you pay separately. Prices below are US list prices checked 18 November 2026, before tax — verify before you pay.

ToolFree planPaid plan (US list prices, November 2026)
ChatGPT$0 — limited image creation, slowerGo $8/month; Plus $20/month; Pro $100, $200, or $500/month
Canva$0 — templates, stock assets, and one brand kitPro $144/year (about $12/month billed annually) or $18/month billed monthly; Business $250/person/year or $25/person/month

Three examples to adapt

These are fictional. Replace every detail with your own. A local bakery: six seasonal muffins for $18, Saturday only. Headline: "Saturday muffins, ready by 9." Image: a real photo. Action: "Order by Friday evening." A tutoring service: a free 30-minute introductory session, online. Headline: "A calm first step in maths." Image: a simple illustration of a desk — no real child. Action: "Book a free first session." A handmade soap shop: a three-bar gift set for $24, posted within two days. Headline: "A small gift, ready to post." Image: a real photo of the bars, wrapped as they will arrive. Action: "Shop the gift set."

Mistakes to avoid

  • Letting ChatGPT write the price. It can invent a number. Type it yourself and check it twice.
  • Using an AI image of your product. A customer who receives something different will not come back.
  • Putting everything in the image. If the ad needs a paragraph to explain it, simplify the offer.
  • Testing everything at once. If two versions differ in more than one thing, you will not know what made the difference.

Conclusion

ChatGPT can make designing a simple ad faster, but it does not make the decisions for you: one offer, one audience, one action, and words and images that are true. Start with a short brief, draft the copy with ChatGPT, then edit it by hand — that edit is where the ad becomes yours. Use a real photograph when the product matters, assemble the ad in Canva in the right size, check the spelling, price, link, and platform rules, then test two versions on a small budget.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Can I use ChatGPT to design ads for my business?⌄

Yes, for drafting copy, planning a layout, and creating simple starting images. Under OpenAI's Terms of Use (effective 1 January 2026), you own the output as between you and OpenAI — but it may not be unique, and you must not present it as human-made.

Do I need the paid version of ChatGPT to make ads?⌄

No. The free plan includes image generation, with a limited, slower allowance; OpenAI does not publish a fixed daily number. If you keep hitting the limit, Plus at $20 a month is the usual next step.

Can I use Canva for free to finish the ad?⌄

Yes. Canva Free is enough for a simple ad; Pro ($144 a year, or $18 a month) is worth it only if you make graphics often.

Will Meta label my ad as AI-generated?⌄

Meta may apply an "AI info" label to an ad it detects as AI-created or significantly edited. For social-issue, election, or political ads, the advertiser must disclose AI use.

Can ChatGPT make a logo for my business?⌄

It can generate an image that looks like a logo, but a logo needs to work at tiny sizes and in one color, and an AI-generated image may not be unique or protectable. Use a simple text-based logo in Canva, or work with a designer.

articles.bodyHtml:

AI Tools & Online Business

Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok? How to Choose an AI Assistant for Everyday Business Tasks

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · ai-assistants, business

If you run a small business or a one-person online shop, you have heard four recommendations: Claude for writing, ChatGPT for everything, Gemini because you already use Google, and Grok because it follows X. All four can be useful; none is right for every task.

Most comparisons try to crown one winner. This one treats the choice like hiring: you would not hire four assistants and pay them all — you would list the jobs, interview two candidates on real work, and keep the one that makes your week shorter. This guide compares the four task by task, gives you a one-week test to run before you pay, and covers Meta Muse, a newer agent-style option. Most small businesses do well with one main assistant, plus a second one for a specific job.

A quick map

TaskStart with
Long writing and editingClaude — strong long-form drafting; Projects keep files together
Everyday writing and general helpChatGPT — broadest range: drafting, planning, images, coding help
Email, Docs, and Sheets in Google WorkspaceGemini — built into Gmail, Docs, Sheets, and Drive
Current news and public reactionGrok — live search of public X posts and the web
Simple coding helpChatGPT or Claude — coding help is a core paid feature of both
Images and short video ideasChatGPT or Gemini — both include image tools
Bookings and follow-up errandsMeta Muse — an agent that carries out tasks

Writing and editing: the interview test

Claude is a sensible first test for long writing: drafting and revising longer documents, keeping tone consistent, and working through a document section by section. Its Projects feature keeps the files for one piece of work in one place. The free plan includes standard chat models with limits; the more capable model and coding help are paid. ChatGPT is the flexible all-rounder, often easier when one task turns into several — a product description becomes a social post, then a short email. Gemini is the natural choice if the document already lives in Google Docs, because you can draft, shorten, or summarize without copying text between apps. Grok can draft and rewrite, but writing is not its strongest reason to choose it.

Test them the same way: take one real document and ask each one to tighten it to half its length, then rewrite it for a first-time customer. Keep the version that needs the least fixing. That is the whole interview — the assistant that leaves you the least cleanup wins.

Email, planning, and everyday admin

The deciding factor is usually where your work already lives. If your business runs on Gmail, Gemini has a clear advantage: on the relevant Google Workspace plans it is built into Gmail, Docs, Sheets, and Drive, so you can draft a reply or summarize a long thread without opening another app. ChatGPT suits planning outside one ecosystem: turning a rough idea into a weekly plan, drafting a reply to a difficult customer, or organizing a launch checklist. Claude suits admin involving long material, such as summarizing a policy document or turning meeting notes into next steps.

Use a simple rule before you automate anything: if a task takes you five minutes and the assistant takes four minutes plus two minutes of checking, it has not saved you time. Use AI for the admin you repeat, not the admin you do once.

Research and checking what is happening now

Grok's clearest strength is freshness. It can search live public posts on X and the web, which helps with questions such as "What are people saying about this launch today?" Treat its answers as a starting point: X posts are opinions, rumors, and marketing as often as facts, so verify anything important against a primary source before you repeat it. Gemini is a good choice for research inside Google's world, and ChatGPT also offers web search and deeper research on paid plans. Claude's research feature, on paid plans, suits long documents rather than breaking news. Whatever tool you use, ask for sources, open at least one, and never publish a price, date, statistic, or claim you have only seen in an AI answer.

Spreadsheets and numbers

Gemini is the easiest starting point in Google Sheets: ask it to write a formula from a plain-English description or summarize patterns in a table, all inside the sheet. ChatGPT is useful for work that starts outside Sheets, such as analyzing a downloaded CSV file — upload a small sample first and check it on rows you can verify by hand. Never trust an AI-generated total or formula without checking it, and keep a copy of the original data first. A wrong total that reaches a customer or a tax return is not a small mistake.

Coding help, images, and video

AI coding help suits small, well-defined jobs such as fixing a broken layout or explaining an error message. It is not a substitute for a developer on anything that handles payments, customer data, or security. Coding help is a core paid feature of both ChatGPT and Claude, often chosen for longer work in Claude's case.

For images, ChatGPT and Gemini both include image generation, useful for mockups, social graphics, and blog illustrations. Gemini's higher plans also include video tools, though availability varies. Grok offers image generation on its free plan with limits, but video starts on a paid tier. Claude is primarily a text and coding assistant, so pair it with a separate image tool if images are central to your work. Check the license for any image you publish.

Meta Muse: a fifth option

Meta Muse, launched in the United States on 8 September 2026, is a personal AI agent that can carry out tasks — bookings, shopping, forms, email, and follow-ups — rather than only answering questions. It reached Canada on 18 September 2026, then Japan on 23 October and Singapore on 27 October; its small-business skills are still described as US and Canada only, and Meta has given no date for other countries. It is available to adults 18 and over, and even the free tier asks for a payment card before the agent will act, according to reporting at launch. Pricing reported in November 2026: free with a usage limit (Meta does not publish the free allowance), Power $20/month with 500 million Muse tokens a week, and Maximum $100/month with 3 billion a week. Think of Muse as an errands tool, not a writing or research assistant.

Privacy and data: read this before you paste anything

Check this before you paste business information into any assistant. On ChatGPT personal plans, OpenAI says it may use your content for training unless you opt out in Data Controls or use a temporary chat; Business and Enterprise workspace data is not used for training by default. On Claude commercial plans, Anthropic says content is not used for training by default; on personal plans, a setting controls it. Google says Workspace business data is not used to train models; the same protection does not automatically apply to a personal account. X says it may share public X data and Grok interactions with xAI for training; you can opt out in X settings, going forward only. Muse training on queries is reported as opt-out by default. Never paste passwords, bank details, full customer lists, or medical or legal documents into a personal AI account — and remember that deleting a chat does not undo training that may already have happened.

What does it actually cost?

Prices checked on 18 November 2026 from the providers' own pricing pages and third-party summaries of them. Confirm the live price at checkout.

AssistantFreeMain paid planHigher plans
Claude$0, with limitsPro: $20/month ($17/month billed annually)Max $100/month; Ultra $200/month
ChatGPT$0, with limitsPlus: $20/monthGo $8/month; Pro $100, $200, or $500/month; Business $20–$25/seat/month
Gemini$0, with limitsGoogle AI Pro: $19.99/monthGoogle AI Plus $4.99/month; Ultra $99.99 or $199.99/month
Grok$0, with limits; no videoX Subscription Plus: $8/monthPremium $30/month; Super $100/month; Ultra $200/month
Meta Muse$0, with a limit; card reported as requiredPower: $20/monthMaximum $100/month

Grok's plans changed on 12 October 2026, when xAI replaced SuperGrok with The X Subscription for new customers. Start free, and pay for one plan only when you hit a limit more than once a week. One $20-per-month plan costs $240 per year; two cost $480 — that is the real decision: not which tool is best, but whether a second $240 a year is earning its keep.

How to choose in one week

1. List your five most repeated tasks — replying to customer emails, writing a weekly social post, updating a price list, planning next month's content. 2. Pick two assistants to test. Google Workspace users: Gemini and one other. Mainly writing: Claude and ChatGPT. Following trends on X: Grok and one other. 3. Give both the same real task — a real email, document, or product, with the same instructions, on the same day. 4. Score each result. Did it understand the task? How much did you have to fix? Did it save time after checking? Write the scores down — memory flatters the tool you used last. 5. Test the boring parts: finding an old conversation, uploading a file, exporting the result. You will do these a hundred times; the flashy demo you will do once. 6. Check the privacy settings before you pay. 7. Choose one main tool and one backup, and revisit the choice in three months.

Conclusion

The answer is not the best assistant in general, but the best one for the five tasks you repeat most — and to accept that the answer may be two tools, not one. Start free, test on real work for a week, and check the privacy settings. Pay for one plan when a limit keeps stopping you, and cancel anything you do not use. If an AI assistant is making your day longer instead of shorter, the fit is wrong. Hire for the job, not the brand.

Get help choosing and using AI tools

For personal guidance on choosing the right AI assistant or building a simple AI-assisted workflow, JoJo's Blocks offers AI learning and consulting — email jojobusiness0101@gmail.com.

If you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach new customers through Pinterest, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — email jojobusiness0101@gmail.com. We do not promise guaranteed views, clicks, sales, or results.

Do I need to pay for an AI assistant?⌄

No. All four offer a free plan. Pay only when you regularly hit a free-plan limit or need a paid-only feature.

Which is best for writing?⌄

Claude is a good first test for long documents, ChatGPT is a good all-rounder, and Gemini is easiest if the document already lives in Google Docs. Test all three on the same real document and keep the one that needs the least fixing.

Is it safe to paste customer information into these tools?⌄

Not on a personal account without checking the settings first. Personal plans may use your content for training unless you opt out, while business plans generally do not train on workspace data by default. Never paste passwords, bank details, or sensitive customer data into a personal account.

Is Meta Muse available where I live?⌄

articles.title: Building a Simple Website with ChatGPT: What It Can Do, What It Can't, and a Beginner Workflow
articles.excerpt: Can ChatGPT build a website? A beginner workflow for planning, drafting, and testing a simple site, plus honest hosting options and costs.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Building a Simple Website with ChatGPT: What It Can Do, What It Can't, and a Beginner Workflow
AI Tools & Online Business

Building a Simple Website with ChatGPT: What It Can Do, What It Can't, and a Beginner Workflow

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · chatgpt, websites

You want a website: a page that says what you do, shows a few examples, and gives people one way to reach you. ChatGPT can help you build it, but only in a specific sense: it can plan the pages, write the words, draft the HTML and CSS, and help you fix an error. What it cannot do, in an ordinary chat, is put that website on the internet — there is no "publish" button in a normal ChatGPT conversation. This guide follows one fictional build from start to finish: Ana, a pottery teacher who runs weekend classes and needs one page with the class, the dates, the price, three photos, and an email link to book. Replace her details with yours, and the same workflow builds your site.

What ChatGPT can do — and what it cannot

Separate the work into two parts: making the site, and putting it online. ChatGPT helps with the first, not the second.

It can: plan a site's structure; write headlines, descriptions, and answers to common questions; draft HTML, CSS, and a little JavaScript; explain what each part does; and help you fix a problem when you paste in an error message.

It cannot: host or publish a site from an ordinary chat — the code lives in your conversation until you save it as files and upload them to a host. It cannot register a domain, log in to your accounts, or install WordPress. It cannot guarantee working or secure code: it can write code that looks complete and still has a mistake, a broken link, or a form that goes nowhere. And it cannot process payments, store orders, or keep a live site updated.

A note on ChatGPT Sites

ChatGPT Sites is a separate feature that can build, host, and share a simple website or small web app from a prompt. It has been in public beta since July 2026, and it is not the same as an ordinary chat. As confirmed in OpenAI's own Sites documentation, checked November 2026: Sites is not available on the Free or Go plans; it needs Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, or Edu. Hosting is free through 31 December 2026, and from 1 January 2027 usage above each plan's monthly hosting allowance is billed — Plus includes 125 credits a month, Pro 375, Business 125 per seat. Building or editing a Site counts toward your plan's Codex usage, and a custom domain costs about 25 credits a month on top of what you pay the registrar. A new Site is private by default; where available, you can connect a domain you already own. Each Site's database is capped at 10 GB, and the documentation rules out payment-card data, protected health information, and financial transactions. The January 2027 rates are described by OpenAI as "proposed." Sites can suit a prototype or an event page. For a main business website, the ordinary route in this article is usually safer, because you keep your own copy of the files.

Step 1: Decide what the site is for

Do not open ChatGPT yet. Write one sentence: "This site helps [a specific person] to [do one thing] by [the main action]." Ana's: "This site helps parents nearby find a weekend pottery class and book a place." Then list the sections you need — usually Home, Services, Examples, Common questions, and Contact — and leave out any section that does not help a visitor decide or act.

Step 2: Gather your real content first

Before asking ChatGPT to write anything, collect your business name, one or two sentences about what you do, your services with real prices, two or three real photographs, and your contact details — only what you are happy to publish. This also protects you from ChatGPT's most common mistake: invented details. If you do not give it a price, it may invent one.

Step 3: Plan the site, then draft the words

Ask for a plan first, not a finished site. Give it your business type, your visitor, the one action you want, and your services with prices, then ask for the sections in order and three headline options — and tell it not to invent prices, places, or claims. Ana's prompt looks like this:

"I teach weekend pottery classes for beginners. Visitors are parents nearby deciding whether to book a Saturday class. The one action is to email me to book. Classes are Saturdays 10 am to 1 pm, $35 per person including materials. Please suggest the sections for a one-page website in order, and three headline options. Do not invent prices, dates, places, or claims I did not give you."

Read the plan as a stranger would, then ask it to draft one section at a time, using your facts. Edit by hand: read it aloud, cut slogans, and check every price, date, and name. If a stranger cannot say what you sell and what to do next in ten seconds, the words are not ready.

Step 4: Ask ChatGPT to write the code — and test it

Ask for a single HTML file with the styling included, using the text you approved, the sections in the order you agreed, and a contact section with your email address. Save the result as index.html. If ChatGPT gives you separate CSS or JavaScript files, save those too, in the same folder, with the exact filenames it uses — renaming a file can break the link to it.

Then open index.html in your browser. You should see your site, running locally on your own computer. Nobody else can see it yet — that is normal, and it is the right time to find problems. Check the text, click every link, and make the browser window narrow to see how the page reads on a phone. One warning: a form in a plain HTML file does nothing on its own. It needs a form service or a backend. Do not publish a form that silently goes nowhere — for a first site, a plain email link is more honest than a broken form. If something is wrong, describe it in plain words and ask for a corrected version. Test again until the page works on a computer and a phone.

Step 5: Choose how to publish it

This is the step ChatGPT cannot do for you. You need hosting (somewhere the files live) and, if you want your own address, a domain name.

GitHub Pages — free for public repositories, up to 1 GB per site with a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB a month, custom domain and HTTPS included. One limit matters: GitHub says Pages is not intended or allowed as a free host for an online business, an e-commerce site, or a software service. Ana's class page fits; a shop would not.

Netlify Free — $0, with 300 credits a month as a hard limit for accounts created since September 2025. A deploy costs 15 credits and bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, so 300 credits covers roughly 20 deploys, or about 15 GB of bandwidth, or a mix. When credits run out, sites pause until the next cycle, with no top-up on Free. Personal is $9 a month for 1,000 credits; Pro starts at $20 a month for 3,000. Netlify includes a custom domain with free SSL, allows commercial projects, and lets you drag a folder onto its site — the easiest start.

Carrd — a visual builder for one-page sites, with no code. Free is $0 for up to three sites on a carrd.co address, with "Made with Carrd" branding and no custom domain, forms, or analytics. Paid plans, billed yearly: Pro Lite $9, Pro Standard $19 (custom domain, forms, analytics), Pro Plus $49.

WordPress.com — the flexible option if you want a blog and several pages. Free is $0, with 1 GB of storage, a yoursite.wordpress.com address, and ads shown to visitors; no custom domain or plugins. Paid plans, billed yearly: Personal $4 a month ($48), Premium $8 ($96), Business $25 ($300), Commerce $45 ($540). Monthly billing costs more, and renewal prices are higher. Since April 2026, plugins are allowed on every paid plan.

The domain name is a separate purchase. For a standard .com, typical 2026 prices were roughly $10–$15 for the first year and $15–$22 a year to renew. A domain is rented by the year, not bought outright: if you do not renew it, you lose it.

What it costs

You can build and publish a first simple site for $0. Costs below are US list prices checked in November 2026, before tax — verify before you pay.

ItemFree optionPaid option (Nov 2026)
ChatGPT$0, with usage limitsGo $8/month; Plus $20/month; Pro $100, $200, or $500/month
Static hostingGitHub Pages $0; Netlify Free $0 (300 credits/month)Netlify Personal $9/month; Pro from $20/month
One-page builderCarrd Free $0 (3 sites, Carrd branding)Carrd Pro Lite $9/year; Pro Standard $19/year; Pro Plus $49/year
WordPress.comFree $0 (1 GB, subdomain, ads)Personal $4/month billed yearly; Premium $8/month; Business $25/month
DomainSubdomain onlyA standard .com, typically about $10–$15 first year, $15–$22/year to renew

A realistic first-year budget is $0 for a test site on a free subdomain, or roughly $20–$70 for a small site with a custom domain — the domain plus Carrd Pro Standard ($19 a year) or WordPress.com Personal ($48 a year).

Mistakes to avoid

  • Publishing a form that goes nowhere. Use an email link, or a tested form service.
  • Letting ChatGPT invent your details. Prices, dates, and qualifications must come from you.
  • Choosing the fanciest option first. A shop or booking system is a separate project. Start simple.
  • Forgetting the phone test. Most visitors will arrive on a phone.
  • Not keeping a copy. Save your files somewhere you control — a chat conversation is not a backup.

Conclusion

ChatGPT is a useful helper for building a simple website — as a planner, a writing assistant, and a coding assistant. It is not a website builder, a host, or a publisher. Decide what the site is for, gather your real content, plan the page with ChatGPT, draft and edit the words yourself, ask for the code, test it on a computer and a phone, then publish it through a hosting service you have chosen on purpose. A small site that is accurate, readable, and live is worth far more than a large site that exists only in a chat window.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Can ChatGPT build a website for free?⌄

Its free plan can draft the plan, the words, and the code. Going live is separate: you still need hosting, and a domain if you want your own address. A first site can be published for $0 on a free host.

Can ChatGPT publish my website?⌄

Not from an ordinary chat. ChatGPT Sites is a separate, paid-plan beta feature that can host a site, but it is not available on the Free or Go plans, and hosting above your plan's allowance is billed from 1 January 2027.

Which hosting option should a beginner choose?⌄

For a single HTML page, Netlify Free is usually the easiest start. For a one-page visual site with no code, Carrd is simpler. For a site that will grow into a blog, WordPress.com is more flexible.

What if ChatGPT gives me code that does not work?⌄

That is normal. Copy the error message, or describe what you see, and ask for a corrected version. If the same problem keeps coming back, simplify: publish the simple version first.

articles.title: Canva's AI Editing Tools for Beginners: Practical Ways to Make Better Graphics Faster
articles.excerpt: Use Canva's AI editing tools with confidence: remove backgrounds, erase distractions, expand photos for Pinterest, and know the limits.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Canva's AI Editing Tools for Beginners: Practical Ways to Make Better Graphics Faster
AI Tools & Online Business

Canva's AI Editing Tools for Beginners: Practical Ways to Make Better Graphics Faster

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · canva, ai-editing

Most beginners do not need Canva's AI tools to invent a design from nothing. They need them to fix small things: a cluttered background, a photo in the wrong shape for Pinterest, a stray object in the shot.

Canva's AI editing tools — Background Remover, Magic Eraser, Magic Edit, Magic Expand, Magic Grab, and Magic Media — sit inside the normal editor. Select a photo, describe a change or brush over the part you want gone, and Canva offers a revised version. You still decide whether it is good enough to publish. This guide works through five everyday jobs, following the same fictional candle maker all afternoon.

Before you start

Pick the right size first: Pinterest is usually 1000 × 1500 pixels (2:3), an Instagram post 1080 × 1080 (1:1), a story 1080 × 1920 (9:16). Save your colors and fonts and use the same ones every time. Duplicate the page before an AI edit, so the original survives if the result is worse.

The tools, in plain language

Canva groups its AI features under Canva AI, previously Magic Studio. Names and menu positions change between updates, so search inside Canva for a tool if you cannot find it where you expect it.

  • Background Remover — removes a photo's background in one click.
  • Magic Eraser — brushes away an unwanted object and fills in the space.
  • Magic Edit — changes a selected part of an image from a short description.
  • Magic Expand — extends a photo beyond its edges, so a square photo can become tall without stretching.
  • Magic Grab — lifts a subject out of a photo so you can move it separately.
  • Magic Media — generates a new image from a written description.
  • Magic Resize — reflows one design into other sizes.

Most of these editing tools are paid features. The free plan gives limited AI access; a crown icon or "Pro" label means a tool is not included free. Check what your own account shows before you plan a workflow around a tool.

Job 1: Remove a background

A clean product photo on a plain background works on a website, in a shop listing, on Pinterest, and in a price list. Example: a candle maker sells a lavender candle in a glass jar for $18, photographed on her kitchen table with a dish rack behind it.

  1. Add the photo to a design in the size you need.
  2. Click it, click Edit image, then Background Remover.
  3. Zoom to 100% and check the edges — jar rim, label, wick. If part of the label is cut away, undo and try a photo with more contrast.
  4. Add a plain background — a busy pattern competes with the product.
  5. Add the price and one short line as real text in Canva, not as part of the image.

Export as PNG for a transparent background, or JPG for a solid one. It works best on one product in good light; it struggles with hair, fur, glass, and thin edges.

Job 2: Clean up a photo

Magic Eraser removes small things that should not be there: a power cable, a price sticker, a stranger in the background. Take the same candle photo, but now a spoon lies next to the jar.

  1. Click the photo, choose Edit image, then Magic Eraser.
  2. Pick a brush slightly larger than the object.
  3. Brush over the spoon in one slow pass. Canva fills the area — here, more wooden table.
  4. Zoom in: on a plain surface such as wood or sky the repair is often invisible, but on a busy pattern such as tiles it can look smeared.
  5. If it looks wrong, undo and try a smaller brush, or crop the object out. Cropping is often faster and cleaner.

Do not use this tool to change what a photo honestly shows: removing a spoon is tidying up, removing a crack or a warning label is misleading a buyer.

Job 3: Change one part of an image

Magic Edit changes part of an image without starting over. Example: a bakery's gift box of biscuits, photographed on a plain table in November, needs a simple festive touch for December without restyling the scene.

  1. Click the photo, choose Edit image, then Magic Edit.
  2. Brush over the area to change — the background only, not the product.
  3. Type one short description: "plain warm cream background with a few small pine sprigs at the edges, soft daylight, no text." One change at a time works better than three.
  4. Compare the versions and pick the most natural one, checking at full size for warped letters, a changed product shape, or shadows pointing in two directions.
  5. If none is good enough, try once more with a simpler description; if it still fails, use a real photo or a plain background.

Do not use Magic Edit to change a real product — its color, label, or shape. A customer who orders the edited version and receives the real one will feel misled.

Job 4: Fit a photo to a new shape

This saves the most rework for Pinterest. You have a good square photo and need a tall 2:3 graphic. Stretching looks wrong; cropping cuts off the edges. Magic Expand adds new image around the original instead. Example: a plant shop's window display, square, with the sign at the top and plants below. Add the photo to a 1000 × 1500 pixel design, click it, choose Crop or Edit image, then Magic Expand (its location has moved between updates, so search for "Expand" if needed). Choose the new size — here, the whole page. Canva usually offers four versions: compare them. Does the new sky match the old sky? Does a plant continue naturally? Does the sign stay straight? Put your headline over the new, plain areas, not over the original photo, so the text is readable. Magic Expand works best when the photo's edges are simple — sky, a plain wall, grass. It struggles when an edge cuts through a face, a hand, or text; if it looks wrong, try a smaller expansion or a plain color block.

Job 5: Generate a supporting image

Magic Media generates an image from a written description. It suits a supporting image — a background texture, a simple illustration, or a scene that is hard to photograph — but not a real photo of your product, shop, or yourself. Example: a tutoring service needs a calm image for a post about planning a study week. A generated image of a tidy desk with a notebook, a pencil, and a cup of tea, in soft daylight, with no text and no people, is a reasonable starting point. Open Magic Media and describe the scene, colors, and light — and what to leave out. Add "no text, no people, no logos", as AI tools often produce garbled words. Check each version at full size — hands, faces, text, numbers, and product shapes are where AI images most often go wrong. If an image has an error, generate a new version, simplify the prompt, or use a real photo instead. Check the license: under Canva's AI Product Terms, as reported in 2026, you may use the output commercially, but it may not be unique, and you cannot sell an AI image on a standalone basis — it must be part of a larger design. Purely AI-generated images have uncertain copyright protection in the US, and Canva's IP indemnity (Canva Shield) is Enterprise-only. Read Canva's terms yourself before using AI images in a product you sell. Use generated images for decoration, and real photos for anything a customer will judge you by.

When AI makes it worse

Not every edit is an improvement, and knowing when to stop is part of the skill. Walk away from the AI result when the edges look melted (Background Remover on glass, hair, or fur often leaves a halo — a plain-background photo taken properly beats a rescued one), when the fill looks smeared (Magic Eraser on a busy pattern such as tiles usually shows — crop instead), when the product changed shape (Magic Edit can quietly widen a jar or change a color — if the product in the image is not the product you ship, do not publish it), or when the expanded area invents things (Magic Expand sometimes adds a plant or a shadow that was never there). The test is always the same: zoom to 100%, look at it on a phone as well as a computer, and ask whether a customer would notice. If you can see the edit, so can they.

What it costs, and when Pro is worth it

Canva Free ($0) covers the editor, many templates and stock assets, and limited AI access, with 5 GB of storage. Canva Pro, for one person, costs US$144 a year (US$12 a month, billed yearly) or US$18 a month, in the US, before tax, as shown on Canva's pricing page in October 2026. Pro includes 100 GB of storage, more templates and premium assets, more brand kits, and the AI editing tools in this guide. Canva Business costs US$250 a person a year or US$25 a person a month. The AI allowance is shared across Canva's AI tools, and heavier tools use more of it: Pro gets about 10 times the Free allowance, and Business about 20 times. Exact per-plan counts are not published as a fixed table on Canva's public pricing page, so check your remaining allowance in your account rather than planning around a number quoted in an article. Pro is worth it when you do these jobs every week and the free allowance keeps running out — not for one graphic a month.

Conclusion

Canva's AI editing tools are at their best on small, specific jobs: removing a background, erasing one distraction, extending a photo to fit Pinterest, or changing one part of an image. They save time by removing the fiddly work, not the thinking. You still choose the photo, write the words, and check the result — at full size, on a phone, before anyone else sees it.

Start with one tool and one job — Background Remover on a single product photo is the best first test — check the result at full size, and save that design as a template.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use Canva's AI editing tools for free?⌄

Yes, with limits. The free plan includes limited AI access, but most editing tools in this guide are paid features, so check what your own account shows.

Do I need Canva Pro to remove a background?⌄

For regular use, yes. Background Remover is a Pro feature, and you should not plan a regular workflow around a free allowance you have not checked.

Will Magic Eraser or Magic Edit change my product?⌄

They can. Both can change shapes, edges, and details, so check the edited area at full size and do not use them to change what a product actually looks like.

Can I use AI-generated images from Canva commercially?⌄

Under Canva's AI Product Terms, as reported in 2026, you may use the output commercially, but you cannot sell an AI image on a standalone basis — it must be part of a larger design. The output may not be unique, and purely AI-generated images have uncertain copyright protection in the US.

Is Canva AI a replacement for Photoshop?⌄

No. Canva's AI tools are faster and easier for simple edits, but they do not offer the precision, layers, or control of a professional photo editor.

How many AI edits can I make each month?⌄

It depends on your plan: Pro gets about 10 times the Free allowance and Business about 20 times. Check your remaining allowance in your Canva account.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Freelance Services Beginners Can Offer (Without Faking Expertise)
articles.excerpt: Start freelancing with AI the honest way: seven beginner services, real Upwork and Fiverr fees, sample-building tips, and pricing that respects your time.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. AI-Assisted Freelance Services Beginners Can Offer (Without Faking Expertise)
AI Tools & Online Business

AI-Assisted Freelance Services Beginners Can Offer (Without Faking Expertise)

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · freelancing, ai-services

Picture the email. A candle maker in your town writes: "I have five scents and a price list. Can you write the product descriptions?" You can write clearly, you have used a chatbot a few times, and the job would take an afternoon.

The temptation is to paste her notes into an AI tool and send back whatever comes out. The result would read smoothly, get two of the five prices wrong, and cost you the client and the referral she would have given you.

AI-assisted freelancing is not about the AI. It is about selling a real skill you already have — clear writing, careful research, staying organized — and using AI to do that skill faster. This guide shows you seven services a beginner can honestly offer, how to prove you can do them, where to find the first client, and what to charge. It promises no income. Freelance income is possible, never guaranteed, and usually starts slowly. The rule: you are in charge at every step. You decide what the client needs, you give the AI clear instructions, you check everything it produces, and you fix what is wrong before the client sees it.

Three things AI gets wrong

Facts. AI invents names, dates, prices, and statistics that sound confident and are wrong. Every claim in client work gets checked against a reliable source — the client's own price list, the business's website, an official page — or it gets cut.

Voice. AI writing sounds smooth and generic. A candle maker, a plant shop, and a plumber should not sound like the same person. Your job is to make the words fit the business, not to deliver the chatbot's default tone.

Honesty. If a client asks whether you used AI, say so plainly — ideally before you start. Never present AI output as your own original research, never claim a qualification you do not hold, and never use AI for work where a mistake could harm someone, such as medical, legal, or financial advice, unless you are qualified in that field.

Seven services you can realistically offer

Pick one. Not three, not seven — one, until you have done it for a paying client.

1. Research and clear summaries

"Find three scheduling tools for a two-person salon, compare prices and features, and give me a one-page summary." AI can organize your notes and draft the page. The checking is yours: when two sources disagree on a price, say so instead of picking the number that looks tidier.

2. Drafting and editing short written work

The client supplies the facts; you turn them into a clear draft. Our candle maker sends five scents and prices; you write a short description for each, all in the same tone.

3. Social media drafting support

A plant shop sends four photos and a note that a delivery arrives Friday. You draft three posts: one announcing the delivery, one explaining how to care for a single plant, one asking followers which plant they would choose. Check the names, prices, and opening hours, and never invent a sale the shop is not running.

4. Admin and virtual assistant support

Sorting an inbox, replying to routine emails from an approved template, updating a spreadsheet, booking appointments, turning a meeting recording into action items. Two rules: do not send anything the client has not approved, and do not paste a client's emails into an AI tool if they said not to. For a deeper guide, see AI-Assisted Virtual Assistant Work.

5. Transcription, captions, and repurposing

Use AI transcription for the first pass, then correct it by hand. A 20-minute talk becomes a transcript, captions, and three short quotes. AI still mishears names and numbers, and a transcript with the wrong price is worse than no transcript at all. For a fuller guide, see AI Transcription, Captioning and Repurposing.

6. Simple design support with Canva

If you are not a trained designer, do not sell yourself as one. Offer simple support instead: turning a client's text and photos into a tidy graphic, a Pinterest pin, or a price list, using Canva templates. Check every AI-edited image at full size before delivery.

7. Spreadsheet and data cleanup

"Our product list has 80 rows, some prices are out of date, and the categories are inconsistent. Can you tidy it, flag anything that looks wrong, and add a total?" AI can help you write a formula. It cannot decide whether a price is correct. Flag every item you were unsure about and keep a copy of the original file untouched.

Choosing your first service

Write down three services from the list above. Cross out the one you have the least evidence for and the one you would least enjoy doing every week. The one left is your first service. ## Build three small samples before you look for clients

Clients hire on evidence, not promises. Make three short samples from made-up but realistic briefs, and label them clearly as samples: a one-page comparison of three free note-taking tools, with prices checked on the vendors' own pages; three product descriptions for a made-up soap shop, all in the same tone, each under 80 words; and a summary of a made-up meeting, with decisions and action items listed, each with an owner and a date. Check them as carefully as a paid job.

Where to find your first clients: Upwork vs. Fiverr

Most beginners start on a freelance platform, because that is where clients already look for help. The two big ones work differently.

Upwork is where clients post jobs and freelancers apply with a proposal. Each proposal costs Connects: a Basic account is free and includes up to 10 Connects a month; extra Connects cost $0.15 each, and the number needed varies by job. Freelancer Plus costs $19.99 a month and includes 100 Connects. Upwork's freelancer service fee is variable — 0% to 15% per contract, set when the contract starts and shown before you apply or accept. Older guides saying it charges a flat 10% are out of date. Direct Contracts, work you bring to Upwork yourself, carry a 5% fee on Basic and 0% on Freelancer Plus.

Fiverr works the other way around. You create a fixed-price listing, called a Gig, and buyers order it directly. Fiverr keeps 20% of each order, so you receive 80%, including on Gig extras and tips. Earnings are usually available to withdraw 14 days after an order is marked complete, or 7 days for Top Rated sellers and sellers in programs such as Fiverr Pro or Seller Plus.

Both platforms are competitive, and a new profile with no reviews is at a disadvantage. That is normal, not a reason to price your work at almost nothing. Keep first offers small and clearly defined, and ask for a short, honest review when the work is done well.

Pricing your first jobs, honestly

There is no single correct price, and anyone who gives one number for every beginner is guessing. Start with a fixed price for a clearly defined job, not an hourly rate you cannot yet estimate. "Three product descriptions, up to 80 words each, for $30, delivered in three working days, including one round of revisions" is a price a client can compare and accept.

Work backwards from the platform fee. On Fiverr, a $30 order leaves you $24 after the 20% fee. On Upwork, a $30 contract with a 10% fee — one example inside the 0% to 15% range — leaves you $27 before withdrawal or currency costs. If the job takes twice as long as you expect, will you still finish it properly at this price? If not, make the job smaller or raise the price.

A workflow you can reuse for every job

  1. Read the brief twice. Note the deadline, the format, how many revisions are included, and anything the client does not want.
  2. Ask one or two questions, if needed. "Should the summary be one page or two?" beats a finished job in the wrong format.
  3. Agree the scope in writing. What you will deliver, by when, for how much, and how many revisions are included.
  4. Do the work yourself, with AI as a helper. Draft first in your own words, then use AI to tighten it.
  5. Check everything before sending. Read it aloud. Check names, numbers, prices, dates, and links.
  6. Deliver with a short note, saying what you delivered and what you checked, then ask for feedback. If a job goes wrong, tell the client early and offer a fair solution.

What it costs to start

You can start with free tools. Begin with the free plan of one writing assistant, one editing tool, and the platform you choose — and only pay when you can name the limit you keep hitting. US prices below were checked on the vendors' own pages on 18 November 2026; prices vary by country, so check the vendor's page before you pay.

ToolFree planPaid plan
ChatGPTFreePlus, $20 a month
ClaudeFreePro, $20 a month or $200 a year
GrammarlyFree, including 100 AI prompts a monthPro, $12 a month billed annually or $30 a month billed monthly
CanvaFreePro, $144 a year or $18 a month
Otter.aiBasic, 300 minutes a month, 30 minutes per conversationPro, $8.33 a month billed yearly or $16.99 a month billed monthly

If a tool costs $20 a month and you have not earned anything from the work it supports, pause it.

Mistakes that cost beginners their first client

  • Sending AI output unchecked. One wrong price in a product description undoes ten correct sentences.
  • Offering a service you cannot do. "I can do anything with AI" reads as "I can do nothing reliably."
  • Pricing so low you resent the work. A $5 job that takes three hours teaches the client your time is worthless.
  • Hiding AI use. If a client discovers it after the fact, the issue is not the AI. It is that you did not tell them.

Conclusion

AI-assisted freelancing works best when it is honest about what AI does and what you do. AI can draft a first version, organize notes, catch a typo, or suggest a clearer sentence. It cannot understand a client's business, check a fact, or take responsibility for the final result. That is your work, and it is the work a client is paying for. Income may follow, slowly and unevenly, but it is never guaranteed.

If you would rather sell a product than your time, read Selling Digital Products with AI Help. If you would rather build an audience slowly, read AI-Assisted Blogging for Affiliate Income.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Should I tell clients I used AI?⌄

Yes, if they ask, and ideally before you start. Some may ask for no AI use. Agree on this in advance.

How much can a beginner earn?⌄

There is no reliable figure. Most beginners earn nothing at first, then small amounts from small jobs. Treat any income as possible, never guaranteed.

Is Upwork or Fiverr better for a beginner?⌄

They work differently. On Upwork, you apply to jobs and pay Connects to propose. On Fiverr, you list a fixed-price service and buyers order it directly. Try one first.

How much do Upwork and Fiverr take?⌄

Upwork's fee ranges from 0% to 15% per contract. Fiverr keeps 20% of each order, so you receive 80%. Check the current figures in your own account before you quote.

Do I need to pay for AI tools to start?⌄

No. ChatGPT, Claude, Canva, Grammarly, and Otter.ai all have free plans with limits. Start free, and only pay when you can name the limit you keep hitting.
