articles.title: Selling Digital Products with AI Help: A Beginner's Workflow from Idea to First Listing
articles.excerpt: Sell your first digital product with AI help: pick a problem, test the idea, build and price it after Etsy, Gumroad, and Ko-fi fees, then list it once, well.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Selling Digital Products with AI Help: A Beginner's Workflow from Idea to First Listing
AI Tools & Online Business

Selling Digital Products with AI Help: A Beginner's Workflow from Idea to First Listing

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · digital-products, ai-tools

Meet Ana. Every Sunday evening she packs five school lunches. Two years of doing it taught her a system: five days across the top, a shopping-list box at the bottom, a notes space for the things her kids will actually eat. She sketches it on a single page, prints it, and uses it for a month. It works. Then a friend asks for a copy.

That page is a digital product: a file you make once and sell many times — a printable planner, a spreadsheet template, a short guide, a set of social media templates. There is nothing to pack, post, or restock. A file is only worth buying if it solves a real problem, is easy to use, and looks trustworthy.

AI can help you move faster: draft an outline, tidy your wording, write a listing description. It cannot decide what is worth making, check whether your planner works when printed, or know what your buyers need. That part is yours. Income is possible, but never guaranteed, and most first listings sell slowly. This guide follows Ana's lunch planner from idea to first listing.

What counts as a digital product

Start with products that are simple to make, explain, and use. Printables and planners — a one-page weekly planner, habit tracker, meal-planning sheet, or budget worksheet, printed at home. Templates — a spreadsheet for tracking freelance invoices, a simple content calendar, or social media templates, ready to use, with clear labels and no placeholder text or broken formulas. Short guides — a focused PDF on one task, such as starting a balcony herb garden. Design packs — printable wall art or greeting cards, the most competitive category, because they depend heavily on taste; do not start here unless you already enjoy design. Avoid products that need support you cannot give, anything that promises a result you cannot control, and anything that copies someone else's work.

Step 1: Pick a problem you already understand

The best first product comes from a problem you have solved for yourself. Ana did not research "meal planning" in the abstract. She had packed lunches for two years. Ask three questions before you open any AI tool. Who is it for? "Busy parents" is too broad. "Parents who pack school lunches the night before and want a one-page weekly plan" is a real person. What will they be able to do after using it? "Plan five lunches in ten minutes on a Sunday evening" is a promise you can test. What do you know that a stranger would trust? If you have packed lunches for two years, kept herbs alive on a balcony, or tracked freelance invoices for a year, that experience counts. Write the answers in two or three sentences: "For parents who pack school lunches the night before. One page: five days, a shopping-list box, a notes space. Plan the week in ten minutes on Sunday."

Step 2: Check the idea before you build it

Spend thirty minutes checking, not building. Search the platform where you plan to sell — Etsy, Gumroad, or Ko-fi — using the words a buyer would type. Look at how many similar products exist, what they cost, and what they promise.

You are not looking for an empty market. An empty market often means nobody wants the product. Look for a gap you can fill honestly: a simpler version, a version for a narrower audience, or something others leave out. Read a few three- and four-star reviews — buyers often say exactly what was missing. Ana notices that most lunch planners have no shopping list. Hers has one, plus a notes box. That is her gap.

Then check the platform's rules first. Etsy requires digital items to be made or designed by the seller. On 22 October 2026 Etsy tightened its AI rules: AI-generated art is still allowed when the seller plays a clear creative role and discloses AI use in the listing, but AI-generated functional instructions — craft patterns, recipes, and how-to instructions — are no longer allowed, listings made by bots with no human involvement are banned, and most listings now need at least one unedited photo of the real item. Read the current Seller Handbook yourself before listing anything AI-assisted.

Step 3: Outline first, then use AI to draft

Do the thinking before you ask AI for words. Write a one-page outline in your own words: the sections, the order, and one sentence for what each section must do. For a planner, decide the layout first. For a guide, decide the steps first, in the order a beginner would follow them.

Only then use AI as a drafting helper, with a specific prompt that includes your outline. Ana's prompt is not "make me a lunch planner." It is: "Here is my layout — five day columns, a shopping-list box, a notes space. Draft the heading text and the short instructions for printing, in plain language." Then she checks every suggestion against her own knowledge. If a suggestion does not make sense to you, do not use it.

Step 4: Build it, then test it like a buyer

Use a tool you can already manage: Canva for printables and guides, Google Sheets or Excel for spreadsheets. You do not need expensive software for a first product.

Build a rough version, then test it. Print it on ordinary paper at the size you promise. Check that the text is readable, the margins are not cut off, and there is enough space to write in each box. A planner that looks good on screen and fails on paper is not finished. Ana prints hers, uses it for a week, and discovers the notes box is too small for a pen. She makes it bigger and the day columns slightly narrower.

For Etsy, a digital listing allows up to five files, each up to 20 MB, as reported from Etsy's help pages in October 2026 — keep your PDF under that limit, name the file clearly, and check that it opens on a phone.

Step 5: Price it by working backwards from the fees

There is no magic price. Look at five similar products and note their prices. Then work out what you keep. Fees change, so check the current figures before you price.

PlatformWhat you pay per sale (US, Nov 2026)
Etsy$0.20 listing fee, plus 6.5% transaction fee, plus 3% + $0.25 processing. Offsite Ads can add 12% or 15%.
Gumroad (direct sale)10% + $0.50, plus 2.9% + $0.30 processing. Discover sales cost a flat 30%.
Ko-fi Shop5% on shop sales, plus processing (usually around 3% + $0.30). Tips are 0% only if you opt out of Contributor status.

Worked example — Ana's planner at $12:

PlatformFees on a $12 saleWhat you keep
EtsyAbout $1.59About $10.41
Gumroad (direct)About $2.35About $9.65
Ko-fi ShopAbout $1.25About $10.75

These are illustrations, not guarantees, and they exclude advertising and tax.

Step 6: Choose one platform, and list it properly

Choose one platform and learn how it works.

Etsy is the best-known marketplace for printables, and buyers already search there — which also means competition is intense. Listings cost $0.20 and last four months.

Gumroad is simpler to set up and handles checkout, delivery, and sales tax as the merchant of record. Its direct-sale fee is higher, at 10% + $0.50 plus processing, but there is no listing fee or monthly charge.

Ko-fi is the cheapest of the three on shop sales for many beginners, at 5% on the free plan Like Gumroad, it brings little built-in traffic. Ko-fi does not act as merchant of record, so sales tax and VAT are the seller's responsibility.

The listing needs the same care as the product. Write a clear title using the words a buyer would search for, such as "Weekly Lunch Planner Printable for School Lunches." In the description, say what is included, what file format it is, how to print or open it, and how the buyer can contact you. Add a license line, such as "For personal use only — please do not share, resell, or redistribute the file."

Step 7: Launch small, answer buyers, and improve

Publish one listing, not ten. Check it as a buyer would: open it on your phone, read the title and description, and look at the images. Share it in one place where your buyers already are — a relevant Pinterest board, a blog post, or a newsletter. Do not spam it into groups that did not ask for it.

Be realistic about time. A first listing may take weeks or months to get its first sale, and many do not sell at all. That is normal. Diagnose before you change anything: if there were views but no sales, the price, images, or description may need work. If there were no views, the title and the way you shared it may need work. Change one thing at a time. When the first product is genuinely finished, make a second one for the same buyer.

What AI should never do in your product

Do not sell AI output you have not read, checked, and rewritten in your own voice. Do not sell a guide whose facts you have not verified, a planner you have not printed, or a template whose formulas you have not tested. Do not copy another seller's work, and do not ask AI to rewrite someone else's work "in different words" — that is still copying. Do not use images, fonts, or illustrations unless you know you have the right to sell them: a free download is not the same as a commercial license.

Conclusion

Ana's planner did not make her rich. It sold a few copies in its first month, then a few more when she pinned it properly, and the second product — the monthly version for the same buyers — sold better than the first, because she already knew who she was making it for. That is what it actually looks like: choose a small problem you understand, check that someone wants it solved, outline the product yourself, use AI to draft and tidy, build it carefully, test it like a buyer, price it after fees, and list it once, properly. Most beginners will not earn much from a first product, and some will earn nothing.

If you would rather sell your time than a file, read AI-Assisted Freelance Services Beginners Can Offer. If you would rather sell a physical product made from your designs, read Starting a Print-on-Demand Shop with AI Design Help.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a paid AI subscription to make a digital product?⌄

No. ChatGPT, Claude, and Canva all have free plans. Only pay when you can name the limit you keep hitting.

Which platform is best for a beginner — Etsy, Gumroad, or Ko-fi?⌄

It depends on how buyers will find you. Etsy has the most built-in search traffic but the most competition. Gumroad and Ko-fi are simpler and cheaper to start, but bring less built-in traffic. Start with one, not all three.

How much can I earn from my first digital product?⌄

There is no reliable figure. Most first products earn nothing at first, then small amounts if the product is useful and people can find it. Treat any income as possible, never guaranteed.

Can I use AI art in an Etsy listing?⌄

Yes, if you played a clear creative role and say in the listing description that AI was used. AI-generated patterns, recipes, and instructions are not allowed on Etsy, and listings made by bots with no human involvement are banned. Check the Seller Handbook before you list.

articles.title: AI Short-Form Video as a Side Hustle: A Realistic Guide to Shorts, Reels and TikTok
articles.excerpt: Short-form video as a side hustle, honestly: Shorts, Reels, and TikTok payouts, the 2027 YouTube changes, AI labeling, and a weekly workflow.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. AI Short-Form Video as a Side Hustle: A Realistic Guide to Shorts, Reels and TikTok
AI Tools & Online Business

AI Short-Form Video as a Side Hustle: A Realistic Guide to Shorts, Reels and TikTok

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · short-form-video, side-hustle

You have seen the video: a creator films a 40-second clip, it gets a million views, and the caption says they made rent from it. What the caption leaves out is the 60 videos before it that got 200 views each.

Short-form video looks like the easiest side hustle there is: a phone, a 40-second clip, and a platform that might show it to thousands of strangers. That is true, and it is also why so many people post for two weeks and stop. The filming is the easy part. The hard part is making something a stranger wants to finish, doing it again the next day, and waiting before any money appears.

This guide covers how the three platforms actually work, what AI can usefully do, and what it costs — including the YouTube rule changes coming on 1 February 2027. Income is possible, but never guaranteed, and for most beginners it starts small and slow.

Pick one audience before you open any app

A short video is not a product. It is a free sample of your attention, your taste, or your knowledge. The money, when it comes, usually comes from platform payouts, brand deals, affiliate links, or your own product. Platform payouts are the slowest and least predictable of the four, yet they are the one most beginners plan around. That is backwards.

Start with the audience, not the platform. "Short videos for busy parents who pack school lunches" is a promise you can keep. Write your one-sentence audience down, and check every video idea against it.

The three platforms, side by side

All three want the same thing — vertical video, 1080 × 1920 pixels, that holds a viewer's attention — but they pay and distribute differently.

PlatformLengthWhat it takes to earnWhat it pays
YouTube ShortsUp to 3 minutesPartner Program, full tier: 1,000 subscribers and 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days, or 4,000 watch hours on long videos in 12 months.Creators keep 45% of allocated Shorts revenue. Reported earnings are commonly $0.03–$0.10 per 1,000 views.
TikTokUp to 10 minutesCreator Rewards Program: 18 or older, 10,000 followers, 100,000 views in the last 30 days, a personal account in good standing, based in an eligible country. Only original videos over one minute qualify.TikTok publishes no fixed rate. Creator-reported figures are commonly quoted around $0.40–$1.20 per 1,000 qualified views.
Instagram ReelsUp to 20 minutes uploaded; only up to 3 minutes recommended to non-followersNo per-view program to apply for — the Reels Play bonus stopped offering new deals in March 2023. Gifts open at 500 followers ($0.01 per Star); Subscriptions generally need 10,000 followers.For most small creators, Reels earn through brand deals, affiliate links, or their own product.

YouTube's two doors — and what changes on 1 February 2027

YouTube has two doors into the Partner Program, and beginners usually only hear about the big one.

The smaller door: fan funding only. With 500 subscribers, three public uploads in the last 90 days, and either 3,000 watch hours in 12 months or 3 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days, you can join the expanded Partner Program. This unlocks fan funding — Super Thanks, channel memberships, Super Chat, and Shopping — but not ad revenue sharing. YouTube says this lower tier is not changing on 1 February 2027.

The bigger door: ad revenue. That is the full tier in the table above: 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 watch hours or 10 million Shorts views. From 1 February 2027, new applicants will need 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 qualified watch hours in 365 days or 20 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days.

And the rule that catches existing channels out: from 1 February 2027, even a channel already in the Partner Program needs 10 million qualified Shorts views in the previous 90 days to earn Shorts ad revenue in a given month. Fall below that line and you stay in the program, keep earning from long-form videos, and Shorts revenue resumes automatically when you cross 10 million again.

Examples to adapt: three videos you can steal the structure of

Copy the structure — the hook, the one point, the ending — and fill it with your own knowledge.

Example 1 — the lunch-packing parent (40 seconds). Hook, on camera holding a lunchbox: "You are packing the same three lunches because you are deciding at 9 p.m. Decide on Sunday instead." Then one idea only: show the one-page weekly plan and say, "Five boxes, one shopping list, ten minutes." End with a question: "What is the lunch your kid actually finishes?"

Example 2 — the second-hand bike buyer (50 seconds). Hook, over footage of a bike: "Three things to check before you pay for a second-hand bike — the third one is the one sellers hope you skip." Then three quick checks, each shown: spin the wheels and watch for a wobble, squeeze both brakes, look at the chain for rust. End: "If two of the three fail, walk away."

Example 3 — the faceless desk video (35 seconds). No face on camera. Hands on a desk, a notebook, a pen. Voiceover, in your own voice: "This is my Monday list. Three things, not ten. The first one is the one I have been avoiding." Show yourself writing the three items, crossing off the first, and stopping.

For each of these, the script is 100 to 130 words — that is what fits a 40-second video. Write it, read it aloud, and cut any sentence you stumble over.

The rules that catch beginners out

Label realistic AI content. All three platforms require a label when AI creates or meaningfully changes something realistic — a person, a place, an event, or a voice a viewer could mistake for real. On YouTube, you answer the "altered or synthetic content" question when you upload; since May 2026 YouTube may also add the label itself. TikTok requires its label on realistic-looking AI scenes or people. Meta's rule covers photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio, including a Reel narrated with a realistic AI-generated voiceover. What does not need a label: an AI-written script, captions, color grading, a cloned voice of your own, or clearly cartoon content.

Do not post mass-produced AI clips. YouTube's monetization policies target "inauthentic" content — mass-produced, templated videos with no original insight, commentary, or value added. AI-assisted content is allowed; AI as the entire creative process is not reliably monetizable. TikTok likewise keeps unoriginal or reused material without anything new added out of the For You feed.

A week in the life: three hours, three videos

You do not need a studio. A phone, good daylight, and a quiet room are enough. This takes about two to three hours a week for three short videos, once you have practiced it.

Monday — pick three ideas. Write each as one sentence that promises one thing: "Three things to check before you buy a second-hand bike," not "bike tips."

Tuesday — draft the scripts with AI, then rewrite them in your voice. Ask a chatbot for a 40-second script with a hook in the first three seconds and one clear point. Then read it aloud and rewrite it until it sounds like you talking. Check every fact yourself.

Wednesday — record all three in one session. Film vertically, with the light on your face or your subject, not behind it. Record the whole script in one take, even if you stumble. If you are faceless, film your hands, your desk, or your product, and let the voiceover carry it.

Thursday — edit with AI help, then check at full size. Cut the pauses, add captions, and add one piece of music from the platform's library at low volume. AI captions mishear names and numbers, so read every caption before you export.

Friday to Sunday — post natively, one platform at a time. Upload inside each app rather than cross-posting with another platform's watermark on it. Turn on the AI label if the video needs one.

Sunday evening — review once, and change one thing. Look at which videos people finished and which they swiped away from in the first three seconds. If viewers leave in the first three seconds, the hook is the problem, not the editing. For a fuller guide to the editing tools, see AI Video Tools for Beginners.

What it costs

You can start for $0. A phone camera, the free version of an editor, and the platforms' own music libraries are enough for your first month. US prices below were checked in October–November 2026; prices vary by country and device, so check the vendor's page before you pay.

ToolFree planPaid plan
CapCut$0 — basic editing, auto captions, 1080p exportPro $19.99 a month or $179.99 a year, 4K export, full AI toolkit, 1 TB storage, about 1,200 AI credits a month.
Descript$0 — 60 media minutes a month, 720p export with watermarkHobbyist $24 a month or $16 a month billed yearly (10 media hours, 1080p); Creator $35 a month or $24 a month billed yearly (30 media hours, 4K)
ChatGPTFreePlus, $20 a month

Mistakes to avoid

  • Chasing a viral video instead of a useful one. One video with a million views and no audience behind it earns almost nothing. Ten videos that each help the same hundred people build a channel.
  • Letting AI write the facts. Check every price, date, and rule yourself. A wrong fact in a 40-second video is still a wrong fact.
  • Treating platform payouts as income. They are a bonus that arrives late and varies. A brand deal, an affiliate link, or your own product is income you can plan around — and none of them arrive before the audience does.
  • Planning around the old YouTube thresholds. From 1 February 2027, new applicants need 20 million Shorts views, and existing channels need 10 million every 90 days to keep Shorts ad revenue. Build the audience first.

Conclusion

Short-form video can be a real side hustle, but it is a slow one. The platforms pay only after you have built an audience, and they pay less than the headlines suggest — and from February 2027, YouTube pays Shorts creators only if they hold 10 million qualified Shorts views every 90 days. AI makes production faster, but it does not make the decisions, check the facts, or earn a stranger's attention. Start with one audience and one promise, post three useful videos a week for two months, and label AI content honestly.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Can I earn money as a beginner?⌄

Not quickly. Each platform has thresholds — 1,000 subscribers and 10 million Shorts views in 90 days on YouTube (20 million for new applicants from 1 February 2027), 10,000 followers on TikTok, and no direct per-view program on Instagram — and payouts are small.

Do I need to label AI content?⌄

Yes, when it is realistic. If AI creates or changes a person, place, event, or realistic voice a viewer could mistake for real, turn on the platform's AI label. Scripts, captions, and cartoon-style content do not need one.

How long should a short video be?⌄

For most beginners, 30 to 60 seconds. On TikTok, videos must be over a minute to qualify for Creator Rewards payouts.

Can I post the same video on all three platforms?⌄

Yes, but upload it natively to each one, without another platform's watermark. A TikTok watermark on a Reel limits reach.

articles.title: Starting a Print-on-Demand Shop with AI Design Help: What Beginners Should Know First
articles.excerpt: Start a print-on-demand shop with AI design help: Redbubble vs. Printify vs. Printful, real t-shirt margins, pricing, samples, and copyright mistakes to avoid.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Starting a Print-on-Demand Shop with AI Design Help: What Beginners Should Know First
AI Tools & Online Business

Starting a Print-on-Demand Shop with AI Design Help: What Beginners Should Know First

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · print-on-demand, ai-design

Print on demand sounds like the perfect beginner business: you upload a design, someone else prints it on a t-shirt or mug, and you keep the difference. No stock, no money spent before a sale. That part is true. What the short videos leave out is the margin — often a few dollars per shirt — and that a design nobody can find earns nothing, however good it looks on your screen.

AI can help you move faster: generating ideas, drafting text for a mug, or making a mockup. It cannot judge what is worth selling or whether a phrase is someone else's trademark. This guide follows one t-shirt from idea to sale, with honest numbers at every step. No income promises.

How print on demand actually works

A customer orders a product with your design on it. A print provider prints that one item, packs it, and ships it. You never touch the product. You pay the base cost and shipping, plus the platform's charges, and keep what is left.

Route 1 — a marketplace, such as Redbubble. You upload designs, Redbubble puts them on dozens of products, and buyers find them through its own search. You set a markup — the default is 10% — and that is your margin. You do no marketing, but the margin is small and you have little control over price.

Route 2 — a fulfillment provider plus your own shop, such as Printify or Printful connected to Etsy or Shopify. You choose the products and provider, set your own price, and sell through a shop you control. The margin is usually higher, but you must bring the buyers yourself.

Step 1: Pick a narrow niche you can design for

"Funny t-shirts" is not a niche. "Short, warm phrases for new grandparents who garden" is. A narrow niche tells you what to design next, what words a buyer would search for, and keeps you away from the most crowded searches.

Pick a niche from something you know, then check it before you design anything. Search the marketplace for the words a buyer would type and look at how many results appear, what they cost, and what the best sellers look like. You are not looking for an empty market — that often means nobody wants the product. Look for a gap: a simpler version, a narrower audience, or a phrase nobody has done well yet.

Write it down in one sentence before you open any AI tool. Ours: "Simple, calm gardening phrases for new grandparents, on mugs and t-shirts."

Step 2: Make the design with AI help — then check it like a printer would

Start with your own idea, not the tool's. Write down the exact words, style, and feeling first. "A simple line drawing of a watering can with the words 'Grow slow, grow steady' in a plain serif font, on a transparent background" is a brief. "Make me a gardening design" is not a brief, and the tool will give you a generic one.

Generate the image, then check the words letter by letter. AI tools still misspell words, and a misspelled mug is unsellable. Ideogram is the strongest common tool for text inside an image: its free plan gives 30 credits a week, but only for accounts signed up with Google or Apple — Microsoft and email sign-ups get no free credits unless they later link a Google or Apple sign-in. Everything made on the free plan is public. Plus costs $20 a month, or $15 a month billed yearly. Check the text at full size, letter by letter.

Prepare the file properly. Most providers want a transparent PNG at 300 DPI — commonly 4500 × 5400 pixels for a t-shirt print area. A low-resolution image, or one with a white box behind it, prints badly. Ideogram's free plan downloads transparent images at 1K size; a larger file for print may need a paid plan or purchased credits.

Keep the design yours. AI output may not be unique, and you cannot sell a design that copies someone else's work. Do not ask AI to recreate a famous character, logo, or sports team's branding "in different words" — that is still copying, and marketplaces remove listings for it. For a fuller guide to image tools and licenses, see AI Image Generation for Beginners.

Step 3: Choose a platform and a provider — and order a sample

On the fulfillment route, the provider decides your cost, quality, and shipping time. Base costs vary by provider, garment, color, and size, so check the catalog before you set a price.

Printify is a marketplace of print providers, which usually means lower base costs. Its published start for a standard Bella+Canvas 3001 t-shirt is about $10.98, with US shipping around $4.45. Premium costs $39 a month, or $299 a year (about $24.99 a month), and takes up to 20% off most products.

Printful prints in its own facilities, with more consistent quality, and charges more: about $12.95 for the same shirt, shipping around $4.69. Its Growth plan costs $24.99 a month and becomes free once your yearly sales reach $12,000.

Redbubble works differently: no base cost, no provider to choose. It sets the base price, you add your markup, and it handles printing, shipping, and customer service. The catch is the tier system. Redbubble assigns each account a tier — Standard, Premium, or Pro — based on the quality and uniqueness of the work, not on sales alone, so new sellers are not automatically placed on Standard. Since September 2025 the platform fees are: Standard keeps 50% of monthly earnings, Premium 20%, Pro none. A further 50% fee applies to earnings from markup above 20%, and total fees are capped at $150 a month.

Whichever route you choose, order one sample of your best design before you promote it. It costs one base price plus shipping, and gives you a real photo for your listing.

Step 4: Follow the money on one t-shirt

A standard graphic t-shirt usually sells for $24.99 to $29.99. Below $22 little margin is left, and above $32 sales slow unless you have a real brand. Here is what one sale actually leaves, using a Bella+Canvas 3001 sold on Etsy for $24.99, on the free plans, with US shipping included in the price — so the Etsy fees below are worked on the $24.99 item price only.

CostPrintifyPrintful
Base product cost$10.98$12.95
Shipping$4.45$4.69
Etsy fees$2.82$2.82
What you keep$6.74 (27%)$4.53 (18%)

That margin is before advertising, software, or your time. The Etsy fees in the table are the $0.20 listing fee, the 6.5% transaction fee, and 3% + $0.25 processing for US sellers. Offsite Ads add 12% or 15% when they bring the sale.

On Redbubble the margin is thinner. A $20 base-price t-shirt at 20% markup earns a $4 margin — about $2 after the Standard tier's 50% fee. At that rate, $100 a month takes roughly 50 shirt sales. Do not advertise until you know your margin per sale.

Step 5: List it properly, and tell buyers what they are getting

Buyers cannot touch the product, so the listing must answer their questions. Use real photos and honest mockups — flat and worn, plus your sample photo if you have one. Do not use an AI-generated photo of a person wearing the shirt as if it were real.

Write the title the way a buyer searches: "Grow Slow Grow Steady Gardening Mug for Grandma" will be found; "Cute Mug Design 7" will not. Say what is included and what is not — product, colors, sizes, material, delivery time — and that the item is printed to order, so the buyer understands the wait. On Etsy, add your production partner. Use tags for the niche: ten honest tags about gardening and grandparents beat thirty generic ones.

And remember Etsy's October 2026 AI rules: AI-generated art is allowed when you played a clear creative role and you say in the description that AI was used, but AI-generated patterns, recipes, and instructions are not allowed, and listings made by bots with no human involvement are banned. Check the Seller Handbook before you list.

What it costs to start

You can start for $0: a free plan on one image tool, one design tool, and a marketplace account are enough. US prices below were checked in October–November 2026.

ToolFree planPaid plan
IdeogramFree, 30 credits a week (Google or Apple sign-in only), publicPlus $20 a month ($15 a month billed yearly)
CanvaFreePro $144 a year or $18 a month
PrintifyFreePremium $39 a month or $299 a year
PrintfulFree, $0Growth $24.99 a month (free at $12,000 a year in sales)
RedbubbleFreeNo paid plan — tier fees reduce earnings

The one cost you cannot avoid is a sample order. Do not buy three subscriptions in your first month: one image tool and one design tool are enough.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Uploading a hundred designs and waiting. Ten designs in one niche, listed properly, teach you more than a hundred scattered ones.
  • Pricing from the retail price, not the margin. Work backwards from base cost, shipping, and fees — the table in Step 4, not the price tag.
  • Skipping the sample. A design that prints badly is not a product yet, whatever it looked like on screen.
  • Using trademarked words to get found. Borrowing a brand name or sports team can get a listing removed, and repeat removals can close an account.
  • Treating AI output as finished. Your judgment — the niche, the words, the checking — is what makes the design yours.

Conclusion

Print on demand lets you sell physical products without holding stock, but it is a slow, thin-margin business for most beginners. A few dollars per shirt, a marketplace fee on top, and thousands of competing designs mean success comes from a narrow niche, a few well-made designs, honest pricing, and listings that answer a buyer's questions. AI makes design work faster, but it does not choose the niche, check the spelling, or earn a buyer's trust. Start with one niche, five to ten designs, one platform, and one sample order. If a design sells, make more for the same buyer; if nothing sells after a few months, change the niche or the designs, not the number of uploads.

If you would rather sell a file than a physical product, read Selling Digital Products with AI Help.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Do I need money to start a print-on-demand shop?⌄

No. All three platforms have free plans, and you pay the base cost only when an order comes in. The one cost worth paying is a sample order.

Which platform is best for a beginner — Redbubble, Printify, or Printful?⌄

Redbubble is the simplest start, but the margin is small, about $2 a shirt on a Standard account. Printify and Printful keep more per sale but need you to bring the buyers. Start with one, not all three.

How much can I earn from print on demand?⌄

There is no reliable figure. Most beginners earn nothing at first, then small amounts. A t-shirt typically leaves $4 to $7 after costs on a fulfillment platform, about $2 on Redbubble's Standard tier. Treat any income as possible, never guaranteed.

Can I use AI-generated designs commercially?⌄

It depends on the tool's terms. Ideogram's terms say you may use generated images for any purpose, including commercial use, and Ideogram does not claim ownership of your output. But output may not be unique, and no tool's terms protect you if the design copies someone else's trademark or copyrighted work. Read the terms before you sell.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Blogging for Affiliate Income: An Honest Beginner's Timeline
articles.excerpt: Affiliate blogging with AI help, on an honest timeline: Amazon commissions, FTC disclosure, real first-year costs, and what months 1 to 12 look like.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. AI-Assisted Blogging for Affiliate Income: An Honest Beginner's Timeline
AI Tools & Online Business

AI-Assisted Blogging for Affiliate Income: An Honest Beginner's Timeline

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · blogging, affiliate-income

Affiliate blogging sounds like the simplest way to earn from writing: you write about products you like, add a link, and earn a small commission when a reader buys. A new blog usually takes months to earn its first few dollars.

This guide covers that honest timeline: how it works, how AI can help, what the first year looks like month by month, and what it costs. Income is possible, but never guaranteed.

How affiliate blogging actually earns money

A reader finds your article, clicks a link to a product, buys it, and the seller pays you a percentage of the sale. On Amazon Associates, US commission rates run from 0% to 10% by category. Most everyday categories pay 1% to 4.5%: books and kitchen 4.5%, apparel 4%, toys, home and beauty 3%, grocery 1%, gift cards 0%. Only luxury beauty reaches 10%. Check the live schedule before you quote a rate — rates change.

Two Amazon rules catch beginners out. First, the referral window is short: a reader has 24 hours from clicking your link to buy, or to add the item to their basket — items added in that window still count if the order is completed within 89 days. Second, a new account must generate three qualifying sales within 180 days, or Amazon can close it. Your own orders do not count. Start with one program you understand, not five.

The disclosure rule is not optional

If you earn a commission from a link, you must say so — clearly, in plain language, on the same page, before the first affiliate link. That is the rule in the US under the Federal Trade Commission's Endorsement Guides, updated in 2023. A disclosure buried at the bottom of a long article, or hidden behind a link, does not pass the test. One short sentence at the top is enough: "This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you."

Amazon adds a second requirement: Associates must state that "As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases." Keep both statements on every post with links. A missing disclosure can cost you the account and, in the US, can bring an FTC penalty of up to roughly $50,000 per violation. Disclosure is a legal requirement, not a courtesy.

What AI can and cannot do for a blog

Google does not penalize content simply because AI helped write it. Its published guidance says it rewards helpful, reliable, people-first content however it is produced. What it does penalize, under its scaled content abuse policy, is many pages made mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help readers. Google also stresses manually fact-checking AI output before publishing.

A hundred AI-written pages that say nothing new will not rank, and even if they did, they would not earn a reader's trust. Twenty articles you actually stand behind have a better chance than a hundred you cannot defend.

Examples to adapt: three article shapes that earn trust

Copy the shape, and fill it with a topic you know and products you have actually used.

Example 1 — the honest comparison. "The 3 lunch boxes I actually used for a school year — and which one I would buy again." Structure: one paragraph on how you tested them; one section per product with what it costs, what held up, and what broke; a short comparison table; a verdict that names one winner.

Example 2 — the task guide with links inside it. "How to pack a school lunch your kid will finish (in 10 minutes on Sunday)." Structure: the problem in two sentences; the five steps in order; a short list of the three items you actually use, linked where the reader is asking "which one should I buy?"; a "what I would skip" paragraph.

Example 3 — the single-product review, downsides included. "I used this $28 water bottle for six months: what I liked, what leaked, and who should skip it." Structure: what you bought and why; what happened in month one and month six; three things that worked, two that did not; who it suits.

For each shape, AI can outline the article and draft a first version. Then you rewrite it in your own words and check every fact against the seller's own page.

Step 1: Pick a narrow topic you can write about for a year

A blog earns when readers trust it about one thing. "Products for new parents" is too broad; "simple, affordable lunch gear for parents packing school lunches" is a topic you can cover in fifty articles without repeating yourself. Pick a topic where you already know something and where people spend money.

Before you commit, check it. Search the words a buyer would type: if every result is a big retailer or a magazine, pick a narrower angle. Look for questions with a clear buying intent: "best water bottle for school lunches" is a buying question; "water bottles" is not. Write down twenty article titles before you publish the first one. If you cannot reach twenty, the topic is too narrow.

Step 2: Set up the blog cheaply

WordPress.com offers a free plan with a subdomain and 1 GB of storage; its Personal plan costs $4 a month billed yearly ($48 a year) or $9 billed monthly, and includes a free domain for the first year, 6 GB of storage, and plugin installs. Renewal prices are higher, so check the renewal figure before you buy.

Set up a clear site name, one topic, a contact page, a privacy policy, and an affiliate disclosure page, and connect Google Search Console (free).

Step 3: Publish ten useful articles before you expect anything

The first milestone is not income; it is ten articles a stranger would find helpful. Each one should answer one question properly. Use the three shapes above and rotate between them, so the blog does not become ten versions of the same list. Publish one or two articles a week, on a schedule you can keep for a year.

Step 4: Add affiliate links only where they genuinely help

A link belongs in an article when the reader is already asking "which one should I buy?" or "where do I get this?" Add the disclosure at the top first, then link the product names a reader would need — usually two or three products per article, not twenty. Apply to your affiliate program only when you have something to show: Amazon's three-sales-in-180-days rule means an empty blog with an approved account is a countdown, not a head start.

Step 5: Bring readers with search and Pinterest, not spam

A new blog gets almost no traffic from Google at first. That is normal. A widely cited Ahrefs study found only about 1.74% of newly published pages reach Google's top ten within a year. On a brand-new site, three to six months before meaningful organic traffic is a realistic expectation, and competitive terms can take a year or more. Those are planning estimates, not promises.

Do not wait for Google alone. Pinterest suits a slow blog: a Pin can send readers to an article for months or years after you publish it. Make one Pin per article and link it to the article — not to the affiliate product directly.

An honest timeline for the first year

This is what the first year usually looks like for a beginner who publishes steadily. Timings vary widely, and none of this is a promise.

Months 1–3: building. You set up the blog, publish 10 to 15 articles, and apply to one affiliate program. Income: almost certainly $0.

Months 4–6: first signs. A few articles start appearing in search results for specific, low-competition questions. You may see your first clicks on affiliate links — and, if the timing is right, your first sale, perhaps a few dollars.

Months 7–9: slow growth. The articles that ranked begin to bring a few dozen visitors a week. A first payout may arrive — Amazon pays roughly 60 days after the month the commission was earned, once you reach the $10 minimum for direct deposit. A first payout of $10 to $30 is a realistic milestone.

Months 10–12: the decision point. By now you can see which articles earn and which do not. Some beginners have a blog earning a small, irregular amount; many have earned very little. The honest question is whether you enjoy writing about this topic enough to keep going for another year.

What it costs: the first-year table

You can run a blog for $0 in the first year on a free plan. The table below shows three honest setups, with US prices checked on 18 November 2026. The real cost is time: roughly 100 to 200 hours before the blog earns anything meaningful — which is why picking a topic you enjoy matters more than picking the highest-paying niche.

ItemFree startSimple paid setupPaid setup + one AI subscription
WordPress.com planFree, $0Personal, $48 a year ($4 a month billed yearly; $9 billed monthly)Personal, $48 a year
Domain nameIncluded subdomain, $0Free first year; then $13–$25 a yearFree first year; then $13–$25 a year
AI writing helpChatGPT Free or Claude Free, $0ChatGPT Free or Claude Free, $0ChatGPT Plus $20 a month or Claude Pro $20 a month
Images and designCanva Free, $0Canva Free, $0Canva Pro $144 a year (optional)
Search Console, Pinterest, Amazon AssociatesFree, $0Free, $0Free, $0
Year-one total$0About $48About $288–$432, plus domain renewal in year two

Two warnings. First, the Personal plan renews at $5 a month billed yearly, so year two costs $60, not $48. Second, the "paid setup + AI" column is not better, just more expensive: a $20-a-month subscription does not write better articles, it writes more of them faster.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Publishing a hundred AI-written pages in a month. Google's scaled content abuse policy targets exactly this, and readers can tell when nothing on the page was checked by a person.
  • Choosing a niche only for the commission rate. A high rate on products you do not understand produces articles nobody trusts.
  • Quitting in month three. Three months is when most beginners stop, before search traffic has had time to arrive.
  • Hiding the disclosure. A disclosure at the bottom of the page protects no one and satisfies no rule. Put it at the top, before the first link, every time.

Conclusion

Affiliate blogging with AI help is not a shortcut to income. It is a slow, compounding skill: pick a narrow topic you can write about for a year, publish useful articles steadily, disclose every affiliate relationship clearly, and let search and Pinterest bring readers over months, not days. AI can draft, outline, and tidy, but it cannot use a product, check a fact, or earn a reader's trust. That is your work.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

How long before an affiliate blog earns money?⌄

Usually months. Three to six months before meaningful search traffic is realistic, and a first small payout often comes later still.

Do I need to disclose affiliate links?⌄

Yes. In the US, the FTC requires a clear disclosure in plain language, on the same page, before the first affiliate link. Amazon also requires Associates to state "As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases."

Does Google penalize AI-written blog posts?⌄

No, not for being AI-written. Google rewards helpful content however it is produced, but acts against pages made mainly to manipulate rankings.

How much does it cost to run an affiliate blog for a year?⌄

$0 on a free plan, about $48 on WordPress.com Personal billed yearly, or about $288–$432 if you add one $20-a-month AI subscription.

AI Tools & Online Business

Offering AI-Powered Social Media Help to Small Businesses

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · social-media, small-business

It is Tuesday morning, and Rosa has been up since 5 a.m. Her bakery's Instagram account has not been touched in three weeks. Her phone holds a photo of Friday's sourdough, a customer asking whether she delivers, and a holiday-hours notice she meant to post last month.

That gap is the job: showing up every week for one or two small businesses, turning what the owner already knows into posts that are true, and answering the customers who write in. AI does the slow drafting. You do the learning, the checking, and the showing up.

The job, in one sentence

You help a small business post regularly, accurately, and in its own voice — three posts a week, approved in advance, scheduled on time.

The businesses that need this most have one to ten staff and no marketing person: cafes, salons, tradespeople, independent shops, tutors, local services. They have photos on their phones and knowledge in their heads, and no system for turning either into posts. A small business does not need a viral video. It needs a post that says it is open and what it sells, a post that answers a question customers keep asking, and someone who replies when a customer writes in.

Your first client: a week with Rosa's bakery

Imagine Rosa says yes to a one-month trial: three posts a week on Facebook and Instagram.

On Monday she sends three photos and three facts: Friday sourdough is back, $6 a loaf; the shop closes early on Saturday; a customer asked whether she makes gluten-free bread (she does not). On Tuesday you draft the three captions with AI help, rewrite each until it sounds like Rosa, and check every price and day. On Wednesday she approves two and corrects the third — the wedding is Saturday, not Friday. On Thursday the posts go out. On Friday you check the accounts once, answer the delivery question from her approved answers, and pass the catering question to her the same day.

DayWhat happensWho decides
MondayOwner sends 3 photos and 3 factsOwner
TuesdayYou draft, rewrite, and check every factYou
WednesdayOwner approves or correctsOwner
ThursdayPosts go out on scheduleScheduler
FridayYou check comments once and report backYou

Five services you can genuinely offer

Offer one or two to start.

1. A weekly content calendar. Three posts a week, planned a month ahead around what the business actually does. You draft; the business approves.

2. Writing captions. The owner sends a photo and a sentence — "new sourdough on Fridays, $6 a loaf" — and you turn it into a clear caption with the price, the day, and what to do next.

3. Simple graphics in Canva. A price list, a holiday-hours notice, a Pinterest pin. Use the business's real photos, and put real text in Canva rather than text baked into an AI image, so nothing is misspelled. For a fuller guide to Canva graphics, see /blog/canva-ai-social-media-pinterest-graphics.html.

4. Scheduling and publishing. You load approved posts into a scheduler so they go out on time. Meta Business Suite schedules Facebook and Instagram for free — Page posts can be scheduled from 20 minutes to 29 days ahead — and Buffer covers more platforms on its free plan. Someone still has to watch for comments.

5. Replying to comments and messages. Many small businesses lose customers by leaving a question unanswered for four days. Offer to check once a day and reply to the routine ones — opening hours, directions, "do you have this in stock?" — from answers the owner approved in advance. Anything you cannot answer, pass to the owner the same day.

Learn the business before you write a word

AI can draft a caption in seconds. It cannot know that the bakery closes on Mondays or that the plumber does not cover the next town. Every mistake like that costs the business a customer.

Before you write anything, ask the owner for the facts and write them down on one page: opening hours, what they sell and what they do not sell, prices for the five most popular items, and how to book or order. Ask for five real photos you may use, and which past posts they liked.

Then write three sample posts using only the facts on your page, and show them to the owner. If they say "that sounds like us," you have the voice right.

The weekly workflow

Use the same steps for every client, every month.

1. Agree the scope in writing. How many posts a week, on which platforms, who approves, and what the monthly price is. Put it in a short email, not a handshake. Nothing is published without the owner's approval until you have worked together for at least a month.

2. Gather material once a week. Ask the owner for three photos and three facts from the week.

3. Draft with AI, then rewrite by hand. Give the AI the facts, ask for two or three caption options, then rewrite the best one until it sounds like the business. Check the price, the day, and the opening hours. If the AI added a claim the owner did not give you — "the best coffee in town," "sale ends Sunday" — cut it.

4. Send the week for approval. One message, all the posts, photo and caption together: "Here are this week's three posts. Reply 'yes' and I will schedule them, or tell me what to change."

5. Schedule, then watch. Load the approved posts into the scheduler, then check the accounts once a day. Reply to routine comments from the approved answers, and tell the owner about a genuine complaint instead of deleting it.

6. Report once a month, honestly. One short message: how many posts went out, which ones got the most saves, comments, or messages, and what you suggest next month.

The rules that catch beginners out

Label realistic AI content. If a post uses a photorealistic AI video or a realistic-sounding AI voiceover, the platform may require its AI label. Meta's help pages say so for Facebook and Instagram, for video or audio that was digitally created or altered, including with AI. That requirement does not apply to images, though Meta may still label them itself. Scripts, captions, color grading, and cartoon-style content do not need a label. The test is realism, not whether you used AI at all.

Paid posts are labeled too. Meta automatically applies an "AI info" label to ads it detects as AI-created or edited, and advertisers must self-disclose AI use only for ads about social issues, elections, or politics. If a post is a paid partnership or an ad, say so clearly — use the platform's paid partnership label and plain words such as "#ad".

Never fake engagement. Do not buy followers, use bots to like or comment, or post fake reviews or testimonials. A client who discovers you inflated their numbers will not keep you, and a platform that detects it can restrict the account.

Never post a claim you cannot verify. If the owner did not tell you the price, the date, or the offer, do not write it. If a photo is AI-generated, do not present it as a real photo of the product, the shop, or the owner.

You do not own the accounts. The client owns their Facebook Page, their Instagram account, and their photos. Never change a password without being asked, and never lock the owner out of their own account.

Pricing your first clients, honestly

There is no standard price for this work, and anyone who gives one number for every beginner is guessing. Price by what you will actually do each week, not by what the tools cost. A fair first offer is a small monthly fee for a clearly defined job: three posts a week on two platforms, written from the owner's photos and facts, scheduled and approved in advance, with comments checked once a day. Ad spend is paid by the client, never by you.

Work out what the month is worth to you in hours. If three posts a week plus daily checking takes four hours a week, that is about sixteen hours a month. If the fee works out to less than you would accept for sixteen hours of careful work, the price is too low or the job is too large — make the job smaller before you make the price smaller.

What it costs, and what you actually need to start

You can start for $0. Meta Business Suite schedules Facebook and Instagram posts for free. Buffer's free plan covers up to three channels with ten scheduled posts per channel at a time — a queue limit that refills as posts go out. Its Essentials plan costs $6 per channel per month billed monthly, or $5 billed yearly, so two channels cost $12 a month. ChatGPT Plus costs $20 a month and Canva Pro $144 a year or $18 a month, in the US — but both have free plans, and you should start free.

ToolFree planPaid plan, as checked 18 Nov 2026
Meta Business Suite$0 — schedule Facebook and Instagram postsNo paid tier for scheduling
Buffer$0 — 3 channels, 10 scheduled posts per channel at a timeEssentials $6/channel/month, or $5 billed yearly
ChatGPTFreePlus, $20 a month
CanvaFreePro, $144 a year or $18 a month

Mistakes to avoid

  • Posting without approval. One wrong price or one unwanted photo can end the relationship in a day.
  • Writing in your voice, not the business's. A bakery does not sound like a tech startup.
  • Promising reach or sales. You cannot promise views, clicks, or customers. Promise regular posts, checked facts, and honest reporting.
  • Taking on five clients at once. One client, done well for two months, teaches you the work and gives you a reference.
  • Treating AI output as finished. The AI drafts; you decide. If you would not sign your name to a post, do not publish it under the client's name.

Conclusion

Offering social media help to small businesses is not about the tools. It is about being the person who shows up every week: learning the business, writing posts that are true, getting them approved, scheduling them on time, and answering customers politely. AI makes the drafting faster, but it cannot learn the business, check the price, or earn the owner's trust. Start with one local business, one small monthly offer, and three posts a week done properly. If you want to widen the work later, admin and inbox support is a natural next step — see /blog/ai-assisted-virtual-assistant-work.html.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Do I need experience to offer social media help to small businesses?⌄

No, but you need to be organized, careful with facts, and willing to learn one business properly.

Should I tell the client I use AI?⌄

Yes, if they ask, and ideally before you start.

Do I need to label AI content in a client's posts?⌄

If a post uses photorealistic AI video or a realistic AI voiceover, the platform may require its AI label. Scripts, captions, and cartoon-style content do not need one.

How much should I charge?⌄

There is no single right price. Work out the hours the job takes each month and quote a fixed monthly fee for a clearly defined job.

Can I manage a client's accounts from my own phone?⌄

Only with their permission, and only through the proper access — for example, being added to their Facebook Page in Meta Business Suite. Never ask for, or keep, a client's password.

articles.title: Creating a Small Online Course with AI Assistance: Planning, Recording and Launching
articles.excerpt: Create a small online course with AI help: pick one student and one result, outline, record simply, and compare Teachable, Thinkific, Udemy and Gumroad.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Creating a Small Online Course with AI Assistance: Planning, Recording and Launching
AI Tools & Online Business

Creating a Small Online Course with AI Assistance: Planning, Recording and Launching

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · online-courses, ai-tools

Here is the arithmetic nobody shows you before you record a single lesson. Sell a $49 course on Teachable's Starter plan and you keep about $43.60 after the 7.5% platform fee and card processing — before the $29 monthly plan cost. Sell the same course on Udemy, where a buyer found it through search and paid a $14.99 flash-sale price, and you keep about $5.38. The course is identical. The platform and the price are what change.

That is why this guide starts with the money and ends with the recording. A small online course is one of the most honest digital products a beginner can make: you teach something you already know, in short lessons, and a student pays once to learn it at their own pace. It is also easy to get wrong: the work is front-loaded, and a long course nobody finishes is worse than a short, clear one.

AI can help with the slow parts: turning a messy outline into a clear lesson plan, drafting a script, or tidying up a recording. It cannot know your subject or decide what a beginner actually needs first. That part is yours. Income is possible, but never guaranteed, and most first courses sell slowly.

What counts as a small course

A small course teaches one skill, to one kind of beginner, in a few hours. "How to grow herbs on a balcony" is a course. "Gardening" is not. A good first course is usually 8 to 15 lessons, each 5 to 15 minutes long, adding up to about two to three hours in total, with something to do after most lessons: a worksheet or a short exercise.

Start with a subject you have done yourself, repeatedly — not something you read about last week.

Step 1: Pick one student and one result

Write down, in one sentence, who the course is for and what they will be able to do when they finish it. "Busy parents who pack school lunches will be able to plan five lunches in ten minutes on a Sunday evening." That sentence tells you what to include and what to leave out. Then test it: have you done this yourself, and can you name three mistakes beginners make? If not, narrow the topic.

Step 2: Check the idea before you build it

Spend an hour checking, not building. Search the platform where you plan to sell, using the words a buyer would type. Look at how many similar courses exist, what they cost, and what their reviews say — read the three- and four-star reviews first, because buyers often say what was missing.

Step 3: Outline first, then use AI to draft

Do the thinking before you ask AI for words. Write a one-page outline in your own words: the lessons, in the order a beginner would need them, with one sentence for what each lesson must teach and one thing the student will do.

Only then use AI as a drafting helper. Give it your outline and ask it to suggest a clearer order, spot a missing step, or draft a short script for one lesson you already understand. Check every suggestion: AI can invent a fact or suggest a step that does not work in practice.

A lesson plan that fits on one page is a good test. Take the lunch-planning course: Lesson 1, "The Sunday ten minutes" — teach the five-lunch grid, practice is filling in next week's grid. Lesson 2, "The five formulas" — teach one lunch formula per day of the week, practice is writing five lunches from the formulas. If a lesson cannot be described in two lines like that, it is two lessons hiding in one.

Step 4: Record simply, and check the sound first

You do not need a studio. A phone, good daylight, and a quiet room are enough for a first course. What matters most is sound: students forgive an ordinary picture, but they abandon a course they cannot hear clearly. Record a two-minute test first and listen to it on headphones and on a phone speaker.

Keep each lesson short and in one take where you can. If you stumble, pause, then repeat the sentence — you can cut the mistake out later. Film yourself, film your hands, or record your screen, whichever lets the student see what matters.

Use AI editing to save time, not to replace checking. Descript, for example, lets you edit a recording by editing its transcript. But AI captions still mishear names and numbers, so read the transcript of every lesson before you publish it. If you want to turn recordings into transcripts, captions and clips, see /blog/ai-transcription-captioning-repurposing-service.html.

Step 5: Build the lessons, with practice built in

A course is not a playlist of videos. Each lesson needs three parts: a short lesson, one thing the student does, and a way to know they did it right. The "doing" part is what makes a student finish — a worksheet, a photo of their work, or a three-question quiz is enough. Without it, most students watch two lessons and stop.

Keep the structure the same every lesson: what it teaches, the demonstration, the practice task, and a one-line summary. Add a short welcome lesson and a final lesson that tells them what to do next, and watch the whole course through as a student would.

Step 6: Choose one platform, and work out what you keep

Do not list the same first course on three platforms at once. Choose one. The four common routes are very different, and the cheapest depends on who finds your students. All figures below are US prices checked 18 November 2026; check the live pricing page before you buy.

PlatformHow it worksWhat you pay
TeachableHosted platform; you set the price and keep your studentsStarter $29/mo billed yearly ($39 monthly), 7.5% fee per sale; Builder $69/$89, 0% fee; Growth $139/$189, 0% fee. 7-day trial; no free plan. Processing about 2.9% + $0.30 extra.
ThinkificHosted platform; no platform fee on its own paymentsBasic $40/mo billed yearly ($54 monthly), unlimited courses. 30-day trial, not a free plan. Processing about 2.9% + $0.30 on top.
UdemyMarketplace; Udemy brings buyersFree to publish. You keep 97% of the Net Amount on sales through your own coupon or referral link, and 37% on organic sales. Net Amount is the price after a 3% fee, so a $100 web sale pays about $35.89 organic. List price capped at $199.99.
GumroadStorefront; sell the course as filesNo monthly fee. 10% + $0.50 per direct sale, plus card processing of about 2.9% + $0.30; 30% via Discover, processing included. No course player or progress tracking.

Work out what you keep on one sale before you choose. On a $49 course sold through your own Udemy link, you keep about $46; sold organically at a $14.99 flash-sale price, about $5.38. On Teachable's Starter plan, that $49 sale leaves about $43.60 before the $29 monthly plan cost. On Thinkific Basic, the same sale leaves about $47.28 before the $40 monthly plan cost — but only on Thinkific Payments; your own Stripe account adds a 5% surcharge on Basic.

Step 7: Price it, then launch small

Look at five similar courses and note their prices, then price by what your course does, not by what others charge. A short course of two to three hours sells for $29 to $79 on a hosted platform; on Udemy, the listed price matters less than the discounted price students actually pay. Pick a price you can defend in one sentence: "Two hours of lessons, six worksheets, and a skill you can use this week, for $49."

Publish one course, not three, and check it as a student would: enroll with a test account and try the practice task on your phone. Share it in one place where your students already are — a Pinterest board, a blog post, or a newsletter — with a short, honest description of who it is for.

Then answer your students — a course with an instructor who replies is worth more than a longer course with no one home. Keep a note of every question a student asks: those questions are the next lesson, or the next course.

What it costs, and what you actually need to start

You can start for $0: a phone, a free writing assistant, and a free editing tool are enough. US prices below were checked 18 November 2026; check the vendor's page before you pay.

ToolFree planPaid plan, as checked 18 Nov 2026
ChatGPTFreePlus, $20 a month
ClaudeFreePro, $20 a month or $200 a year
CanvaFreePro, $144 a year or $18 a month
DescriptFree, 60 media minutes a month, 100 AI credits one-time, 720p with watermarkHobbyist $24 a month or $16 a month billed yearly; Creator $35 a month or $24 a month billed yearly

One writing assistant and one editing tool are enough for the first month.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Making the course too long. Ten lessons a student finishes beat thirty they abandon.
  • Recording before you outline. An outline takes an afternoon and saves days of re-recording.
  • Skipping the practice tasks. A course with nothing to do is a video playlist, and students can find those for free.
  • Choosing a platform for its headline price. A $0 monthly fee with a 10% cut, or a 37% share on discounted prices, can cost more than a $29 monthly plan once you sell regularly.
  • Treating AI output as finished. Your knowledge, your examples, and your checking are what make the course worth paying for.
  • Letting AI teach what you have not done. Do not teach a subject you have not done yourself, and do not copy another teacher's course — asking AI to rewrite it "in different words" is still copying.

Conclusion

A small online course with AI help is not a shortcut to income. It is a practical skill: choose one student and one result you can genuinely teach, check that someone wants it, outline the course yourself, use AI to draft and tidy, record simply with clear sound, build practice into every lesson, choose one platform after working out what you keep, and launch small. If a full course feels too big, a single digital file is a smaller first product — see /blog/selling-digital-products-with-ai-help.html.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to be an expert to make a course?⌄

You need real, repeated experience — enough to teach a beginner the steps, the mistakes, and how to fix them. AI cannot supply that experience.

Which platform is best for a first course — Teachable, Thinkific, Udemy, or Gumroad?⌄

It depends on who finds your students. Udemy brings buyers but keeps most of the money on organic sales. Teachable and Thinkific keep more per sale but need you to bring the students.

How long should my first course be?⌄

About two to three hours, in 8 to 15 lessons of 5 to 15 minutes each, with a practice task after most lessons. Shorter and finished beats longer and abandoned.

How much can I earn from my first course?⌄

There is no reliable figure. Most first courses earn nothing at first, then small amounts if the course is useful and people can find it.

Can AI write my whole course for me?⌄

No, not honestly. AI can draft an outline or tidy a script, but it cannot know your subject or teach from experience.
