articles.title: Canva AI for Social Media and Pinterest Graphics: A Beginner Tutorial
articles.excerpt: A tutorial for Canva AI graphics: build a Brand Kit, design with Magic Design, write with Magic Write, and resize one design for Pinterest and Instagram.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. Canva AI for Social Media and Pinterest Graphics: A Beginner Tutorial
AI Tools & Online Business

Canva AI for Social Media and Pinterest Graphics: A Beginner Tutorial

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · canva, pinterest

Most beginners do not struggle to open Canva. They struggle with the blank page: what to make, what to write on it, and how to turn one idea into graphics for Pinterest, Instagram, and Facebook without starting from scratch three times.

This tutorial fixes that with a single workshop. One idea — a one-page weekly lunch planner printable, for parents packing school lunches — becomes five finished graphics: a Pinterest Pin, an Instagram portrait post, a square post, a Story, and a Facebook post. Along the way you will use Magic Design for the layout, Magic Write for the words, Magic Media for a supporting image, and Magic Resize to reformat the finished design.

None of them finishes the work for you. You still choose the idea, check the words, and look at the result at full size before anyone else sees it.

Before you start: set up your brand once

A graphic looks professional when the same colors and fonts appear every time. In Canva, that lives in a Brand Kit: your logo, colors, and fonts, saved in one place. The free plan allows one Brand Kit with up to three colors; Pro allows five and Business allows 100.

Pick two fonts and three colors, upload your logo if you have one, and use only those choices for a month. Canva's AI tools can draw on your Brand Kit, so a layout Magic Design suggests will already look like yours.

The right size first, every time

The most common beginner mistake is designing a square post and then trying to stretch it into a tall Pinterest Pin. Start from the size the graphic will actually be published in. These are the sizes widely recommended in 2026:

Where it will appearRecommended size
Pinterest standard Pin1000 × 1500 px (2:3)
Instagram feed post (portrait)1080 × 1350 px (4:5)
Instagram feed post (square)1080 × 1080 px (1:1)
Instagram Stories and Reels1080 × 1920 px (9:16)
Facebook feed1080 × 1350 px (4:5) or 1080 × 1080 px (1:1)
Facebook Stories and Reels1080 × 1920 px (9:16)

Pinterest rewards tall images: the standard 2:3 Pin takes up more space in the feed, and Pins taller than 2:3 can be cut off on some devices. For Stories and Reels, keep text away from the top and bottom roughly 250 px of a 1920 px-tall frame.

For this workshop, the master design is the Pinterest Pin, 1000 × 1500 px.

Step 1: Turn one idea into a layout with Magic Design

Start with one idea, in one sentence. Not "a post about my shop" but "a Pinterest Pin that tells busy parents about my one-page weekly lunch planner."

Open Canva, choose the Pinterest Pin size, and open Magic Design:

"A Pinterest Pin for a one-page weekly lunch planner printable, for parents packing school lunches. Calm, warm colors, a photo of a packed lunchbox, and the headline 'Plan five lunches in ten minutes'."

Canva returns several complete, editable layouts. Pick the one with the clearest structure — one headline, one image, plenty of empty space — not the busiest one. A layout is a starting point: change the headline to your own words, replace the image with a real photo where the product matters, and delete anything you would not say yourself. If Magic Design has moved in the editor, search for it by name inside Canva.

Step 2: Write the words with Magic Write — then rewrite them

Magic Write drafts text inside your design: headlines, captions, and short descriptions. Give it the facts and a limit:

"Write three headlines of six words or fewer for a weekly lunch planner printable, for parents packing school lunches. Plain, friendly language. Do not add any claims I did not give you."

Pick the strongest line, then rewrite it by hand until it sounds like you, and only says things you can stand behind.

Two rules for text. Keep it short — a headline of six words or fewer, one short line underneath — and use real text in Canva, not text baked into an AI-generated image. Real text stays sharp and editable; text inside an image does neither.

Step 3: Add an image — real photo first, AI image second

For anything a buyer will judge by appearance — food, a product, a handmade item — use a real photograph. A phone photo in good daylight, on a plain surface, is usually better than an AI image.

Use Magic Media, Canva's AI image generator, for a supporting image: a background texture, a simple illustration, or a scene that is hard to photograph:

"A tidy desk with a notebook, a pencil and a cup of tea, soft daylight, flat illustration style, no text, no people, no logos."

Check each version at full size. Hands, faces, text, numbers, and product shapes are where AI images most often go wrong. If an image has an error, do not publish it — generate a new version, simplify the prompt, or use a real photo instead.

If the photo needs a small fix, Background Remover and Magic Eraser can help — both are paid features. Check any edited area at full size. For a fuller guide to those editing tools, see Canva's AI Editing Tools for Beginners: Practical Ways to Make Better Graphics Faster.

Step 4: Make a Pinterest Pin that can be found

A Pin is not just an image; it is a search result. Pinterest works as a search engine for ideas, so a Pin needs words a person would actually type. Put the main idea in the headline on the image itself, large enough to read at a glance on a phone: "Plan five lunches in ten minutes" is readable. Keep it to one or two lines, with strong contrast against the background.

Then write the Pin title and description using the same plain words a searcher would type: "weekly lunch planner printable," "school lunch ideas," "plan school lunches." Say what the Pin leads to and who it is for. Do not stuff it with keywords, and do not promise anything the page behind it does not deliver.

Export the Pin as a JPG or PNG at 1000 × 1500 px, and save it with a clear name, such as weekly-lunch-planner-pin.jpg.

Step 5: Turn one design into every size with Magic Resize

This is where Canva Pro earns its keep for most beginners. Magic Resize takes one finished design and reflows it into another size, repositioning the elements instead of simply stretching or cropping them. It is a Pro and Business feature; the free plan has limited resize options. (Magic Switch is the broader name Canva uses for switching a design's format, size, or language; Magic Resize is the resizing part of it.)

Resize your finished Pinterest Pin into an Instagram portrait post, then into a Story, and check each version by hand: a headline may now overlap the image, or a photo may leave an awkward gap. The resize does the mechanical work; you do the judgment.

A practical rule: make one master design per idea, in the size you care about most, and resize from it. Do not resize from a version that is already a resize.

Step 6: Schedule it, then check it on a phone

Canva Pro includes a Content Planner that lets you plan, draft, and schedule posts to connected social accounts from inside Canva. Before anything goes out, check the finished graphic on your phone, not just on your computer. Read every word, including the price — read the price backwards, digit by digit. Is the headline readable, does the image show what you sell, and is the link correct? Click it yourself.

What it costs, and when Pro is worth it

You can make good social graphics for $0. Canva Free includes 1.6 million-plus templates, millions of photos, videos, and graphics, one Brand Kit, 5 GB of storage, and up to 20 Standard or Premium AI uses a month.

Canva Pro, for one person, costs US$144 a year (US$12 a month, billed yearly) or US$18 a month, in the US, before tax. Pro includes 100 GB of storage, more templates and premium assets, five Brand Kits, the Content Planner, Background Remover, Magic Resize, and a larger AI allowance — up to 200 Premium or 20 Ultra AI uses a month. Canva Business costs US$250 a person a year or US$25 a person a month.

Canva's AI allowance is a single monthly allowance shared across its Standard, Premium, and Ultra AI tools, and harder tools use more of it — so treat the "up to 200 Premium or 20 Ultra" figures as the ceiling, not a promise for every tool.

Pro is worth it when you can name the limit you keep hitting: you resize designs every week, you schedule posts regularly, or you run out of AI uses before the month ends. Prices vary by country, so check Canva's pricing page before you pay.

Licenses: what you can and cannot do with Canva content

Canva's content license allows designs made with its Free and Pro content to be used commercially, including for client work and products you sell — with restrictions around unedited stock media and reselling templates as they are.

For AI-generated images, Canva's AI Product Terms say you own the output and may use it commercially, but the output may not be unique, and you cannot sell an AI image on a standalone basis — it must be part of a larger design. Purely AI-generated images have uncertain copyright protection in the US, and Canva Shield, Canva's IP indemnity, is Enterprise-only.

Four mistakes to avoid

  • Designing in the wrong size first. Start from the size the graphic will be published in, or resize from a master design you already finished.
  • Letting the AI write the facts. Check every price, date, and claim yourself. A wrong price on a graphic is still a wrong price.
  • Using an AI image of your product. A customer who receives something different will not come back. Use a real photo.
  • Cramming too much text on one graphic. One headline, one short line, nothing else. The caption can carry the rest.

Conclusion

One idea, one master design, five graphics. That is the whole workshop: set up your Brand Kit once, turn the idea into a layout with Magic Design, write the words with Magic Write and then rewrite them yourself, use a real photo where the product matters, make the Pin findable, and resize with Magic Resize.

Canva AI is at its best when it does the slow work: turning one idea into a layout, drafting the words, generating a supporting image, and reformatting a finished design for another platform. The decisions are still yours — the idea, the facts, the photo, and the final check. Start with one idea and one size: one master design a week, resized for the platforms you use, checked on your phone.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Can I use Canva AI for free?⌄

Yes, with limits — up to 20 Standard or Premium AI uses a month — but most editing and resizing tools in this guide are paid features.

Do I need Canva Pro to make Pinterest graphics?⌄

No. You can make a Pinterest Pin on the free plan. Pro is worth it when you resize designs often, schedule posts regularly, or need Background Remover and more Brand Kits.

Can I use AI-generated images from Canva commercially?⌄

Under Canva's AI Product Terms, you may use the output commercially, but you cannot sell an AI image on a standalone basis. The output may not be unique, and purely AI-generated images have uncertain copyright protection in the US.

articles.title: AI Image Generation for Beginners: Choosing a Tool, Writing Prompts and Checking Licenses
articles.excerpt: Compare AI image tools for beginners — ChatGPT, Midjourney, Ideogram, and Canva — write better prompts, and check licenses and copyright before you sell.
articles.bodyHtml:

AI Tools & Online Business

AI Image Generation for Beginners: Choosing a Tool, Writing Prompts and Checking Licenses

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · ai-images, licensing

A small business owner who needed an image used to have three choices: take a photo, buy a stock photo, or hire a designer. Now there is a fourth: describe the image in words and let an AI tool draw it in under a minute.

That is genuinely useful — and easy to get wrong. AI images can look convincing at a glance and fall apart on a closer look: extra fingers, misspelled words, a product that is not your product.

This guide answers three questions in order, because the order is the method: which tool fits the job, how do you write a prompt that gives you what you asked for, and what can you legally do with the result? Answer them backwards — generate first, ask later — and you will go wrong.

Question 1: Which tool fits the job?

No single tool is best at everything. Pick by what the image has to do, not by which tool is most talked about:

Do you need readable words inside the image? A poster, a sale banner, or a t-shirt draft with text on it? Start with Ideogram. Most image tools misspell words; Ideogram is the strongest common tool for readable text inside an image. Its free plan gives 30 credits a week to accounts signed in with Google, Apple, or Microsoft (email-and-password accounts get none), and everything made on it is public.

Does the image need to look like art? A book cover, a poster, or a product-page illustration where mood and color carry the message? Start with Midjourney, the tool most often praised for the look of its images: rich color, strong mood, images that feel designed. It has no free plan and no free trial.

Do you already use ChatGPT, or need to edit a photo you own? Start with ChatGPT Images, built into the same chat: describe the image, or upload a photo and ask for an edit. It is on every plan, including Free, but OpenAI describes the allowance in words, not numbers — "limited" on Free, "unlimited and faster" on Pro.

Do you need the image inside a design you are already building? Start with Canva Magic Media, which generates an image without leaving the Canva editor. For the full Canva workflow, see Canva AI for Social Media and Pinterest Graphics: A Beginner Tutorial.

ToolBest forPaid plans, as reported Nov 2026
ChatGPT ImagesEveryday illustrations, photo editsFree, limited; Go $8/mo; Plus $20/mo; Pro from $100/mo
MidjourneyArtistic images, postersNo free plan; Basic $10; Standard $30; Pro $60; Mega $120/mo
IdeogramImages with readable textFree, 30 credits/week, public; Plus $20 ($15 yearly); Pro $60 ($42 yearly)/mo
Canva Magic MediaImages inside CanvaFree, limited allowance; Pro $144/yr or $18/mo; Business $250/yr

Start with one tool — the one you already pay for, if any. Add a second only when you can name a job the first keeps failing at.

What AI images are good for — and what they are not

AI image tools turn a written description into a picture. They are good at supporting images: a background texture, a simple illustration for a blog post, or a scene that is hard to photograph.

They are a poor choice for anything a buyer will judge by appearance. An AI image of a cake is not your cake, and an AI photo of a person wearing your shirt is not a real customer. For food, products, handmade goods, and real people, use a real photograph. They are also the wrong tool for exact facts: if the image must show a specific price, a real place, a logo, or a person's face, do not generate it.

Question 2: How do you write a prompt that works?

A good prompt is a brief, not a wish. Give the tool six things: subject, action, setting, style, light, and what to leave out. A plant shop wants an image for a post about caring for herbs:

"Three small potted herbs — basil, mint and parsley — in plain terracotta pots on a light wooden table, near a window, soft daylight, flat illustration style, warm colors, no text, no people, no logos."

Each part earns its place — and "no text, no people, no logos" rules out the three things AI images most often get wrong.

The prompt lab: three habits that fix most failures

Describe the scene, not the finished design. "A calm morning desk" gives the tool room to compose. "A Pinterest Pin with a headline in the top third" asks an image generator to do a designer's job, badly. Write the headline yourself, in real text, in Canva — never baked into the image.

Change one thing at a time. If the image is wrong, change one element — the style, or the light, or one object — and generate again.

Keep a note of prompts that worked. Save the prompt with the image file. Six months later, it is the only way to repeat the style.

Do not put a real person's name, a brand name, a trademarked character, or a famous logo in a prompt.

The five-point check: look at every image at full size

Check every image at 100% zoom before anyone else sees it. Five things to check:

Hands and faces. Extra fingers, a hand with the wrong number of joints, a face that looks almost right but not quite — the most common errors. If a hand looks wrong, crop it out or generate a new version.

Text. Read every word, letter by letter. AI tools still misspell words or invent words that look real at a glance. Never skip this check, even from Ideogram.

Numbers, shadows, and logic. Count the objects: three herbs, not four. Shadows pointing in two directions or a cup floating above a table are small impossibilities that make an image feel wrong.

Would a customer be misled? Would a reasonable person think it is a real product, place, or person? If yes, do not use it as if it were a photograph.

If an image fails, generate a new version, simplify the prompt, or use a real photo.

Question 3: What can you legally do with it? The license clinic

Three questions, in order. This is a summary of reported terms, not legal advice. For a specific product or dispute, ask a lawyer where you live.

1. Does the tool allow commercial use? Most paid plans do, but the details differ. OpenAI's terms say you own the output — but it may not be unique, and you must not present it as human-made. Midjourney says you own the assets you create, but companies earning over $1,000,000 a year must be on Pro or Mega to own them. Ideogram does not claim ownership of your outputs and does not restrict commercial use. Canva says you own the output and may use it commercially, but you cannot sell an AI image on its own. Read the terms of the tool you use before you sell anything made with it.

2. Do you own the copyright? Probably not — at least, not in the image alone. In the United States, copyright requires a human author. The US Copyright Office's January 2025 report concluded that prompts alone do not make the user the author, the D.C. Circuit agreed in Thaler v. Perlmutter (March 2025), and the Supreme Court declined to revisit it (2 March 2026). What you add can be protected: your own drawing, edits, or arrangement with your own text. A purely AI-generated image is unlikely to be protected. Do not build your brand's core asset — a logo, a book cover, a product's main image — from one unedited AI image.

3. Does the image copy someone else's work? An AI image can reproduce a recognizable style, a trademarked character, or a protected design. If the image looks like a famous character, a real person's face, or a well-known logo, do not use it. A free download is not a commercial license.

Putting the image to work

An image earns its keep when it does a job. Three common ones for a beginner.

A Pinterest Pin. Pinterest rewards tall images — the standard Pin is 1000 × 1500 pixels (2:3). Add your headline as real text in Canva.

A product mockup. An AI image can show a design on a mug or a t-shirt for a first listing, but replace it with a real photo of the printed product as soon as you have one.

What it costs, and when paying is worth it

You can start for $0: ChatGPT, Ideogram, and Canva all have free plans. US prices below were reported in October–November 2026, before tax. ChatGPT: Go $8, Plus $20, Pro from $100 a month. Midjourney: Basic $10, Standard $30, Pro $60, Mega $120 a month, about 20% less billed yearly. Ideogram: Plus $20 ($15 yearly), Pro $60 ($42 yearly) a month. Canva: Pro $144 a year or $18 a month.

Pay only when you can name the limit you keep hitting. Do not pay for three tools in your first month: one image tool and one design tool are enough.

Six mistakes to avoid

  • Using an AI image of your product. A customer who receives something different will not come back. Use a real photo.
  • Presenting an AI image as a real photo. An illustration is honest when it looks like one.
  • Skipping the full-size check. Hands, text, and shadows fail at full size, not as a thumbnail.
  • Assuming you own the copyright. A prompt alone does not make you the author under US law. Add your own work.
  • Copying someone else's work through a prompt. Asking for a famous character, logo, or brand "in different words" is still copying.
  • Paying for four tools at once. One tool, used well for a month, teaches you more.

Conclusion

AI image generation is at its best on small, specific jobs: a supporting illustration, a background texture, a first draft, or a Pinterest image in the right shape. It saves time by removing the slow work, not the thinking. You still choose the image, write the prompt, check the result at full size, and check the license before you publish or sell it.

Start with one tool you already have, one prompt formula, and one honest check: would a customer be misled by this image, and do I have the right to use it this way? If either answer is unsure, fix it first.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Which AI image tool should a beginner start with?⌄

The one you already have — ChatGPT or Canva. Add Ideogram for readable text, and Midjourney when the artistic look is the point.

Can I use AI-generated images commercially?⌄

Usually yes, under the tool's terms — but the details differ by tool, and the terms change. Check them before you sell anything.

Do I own the copyright in an AI image I generated?⌄

Probably not in the image alone. In the US, copyright requires a human author, and prompts alone do not make you the author. What you add — your own artwork, edits, or arrangement with your own text — can be protected.

Why does my AI image have misspelled words or extra fingers?⌄

Because the tool predicts what a picture should look like; it does not understand words or count fingers. Check every image at full size.

Can I use an AI image as my logo?⌄

It is a poor choice. A logo needs to work at tiny sizes and in one color, an AI image may not be unique, and you are unlikely to own the copyright in it.

articles.title: AI Video Tools for Beginners: Editing, Captions and Short-Form Clips
articles.excerpt: Edit your short video with AI: CapCut or Descript for editing, captions people can read, and OpusClip to cut clips from long videos. Honest costs included.
articles.bodyHtml:
1. Home
  2. Blog
  3. AI Video Tools for Beginners: Editing, Captions and Short-Form Clips
AI Tools & Online Business

AI Video Tools for Beginners: Editing, Captions and Short-Form Clips

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · ai-video, editing

Your first short video does not need a studio, a course, or a second mortgage in subscriptions. It needs a phone, one clear sentence, and about an afternoon. The sentence is the video. Everything else — the cuts, the captions, the clips — is just removing the parts that get in its way.

That is where AI video tools actually help. They are not directors. They are fast, tireless assistants for the boring jobs: cutting out the pauses, typing out the captions, and finding the two minutes inside a 45-minute recording that can stand on their own. This guide walks you through those three jobs in order, with the costs, the limits, and the one job — generating video from nothing — where beginners should slow down.

Your first video in an afternoon

Here is the whole job, before we get into tools. You are making a 40- to 60-second vertical video that answers one question or shows one thing. Write one sentence that states the promise, then write 100 to 130 words that deliver it. That is your script. Film it in one take, in daylight, with the light on your face or your subject, not behind it.

Then the edit takes roughly an hour the first time, and much less after that:

  1. Cut the pauses first. Remove silences, false starts, and filler words. This alone usually cuts a third of the length and makes the video feel twice as fast.
  2. Add captions, then read them. Auto-captions give you a draft. You give them a proofread.
  3. Add one quiet piece of music from the platform's own library, under your voice.
  4. Export vertical, 1080 × 1920 (9:16), at 1080p. Watch it on your phone with the sound off. If the point is not clear without sound, the captions or the visuals need work, not the music.

If that sounds doable, it is. The rest of this guide is choosing the tool that makes those four steps easiest for the way you record.

Step 1: Pick one editor and learn it properly

Do not sign up for four tools in your first month. Pick one, use it for ten videos, and only then judge it.

CapCut — the easiest start for short-form video. CapCut is a timeline editor built for vertical video, on phone, desktop, and web. You cut clips on a timeline, add captions, music, text, and effects, and export in the right size for each platform. It suits a beginner who records on a phone and posts Shorts, Reels, or TikTok. Its AI tools include auto-captions, background removal, and text-to-video, and the AI features run on credits on paid plans.

Descript — the best start if you talk to camera. Descript edits video by editing its transcript: delete a sentence and the video cuts itself. It suits tutorials and lessons, where the words matter most, and it has Studio Sound and filler-word removal. If you film your hands or your product rather than your face, CapCut is the better fit.

Step 2: Captions people can actually read

Captions are where most beginner videos fail, and they are the easiest thing to fix. Most viewers watch with the sound off, so captions are not optional — they are the video for a large part of your audience.

AI captions get the words roughly right and the details wrong, so the check matters more than the generation. Read every caption while watching the video. Each caption should appear when the words are spoken, stay on screen long enough to read, and break at a natural pause. Keep lines short — about 42 characters at most — and no more than two lines at a time.

Check the names, numbers, and prices first. AI captions mishear all three, and a caption with the wrong price is a wrong price. Use a plain, bold font in white with a dark outline or background, so the words stay readable over any part of the video. And keep captions in the middle of the frame: the top and bottom edges are covered by usernames, buttons, and platform captions, so text parked there disappears.

Step 3: Turn one long video into short clips

If you already record long videos — a lesson, a podcast, a talk — the cheapest way to make short-form content is to cut clips from them, not to record new ones.

Upload the long video to a clipping tool such as OpusClip. It finds the moments that stand alone — a clear answer to a common question, a short story, a surprising fact — reframes them vertically, adds captions, and gives each clip a score. A 45-minute recording can become three to five usable clips.

Then do the part the tool cannot do. Watch each clip yourself, from start to finish. Does it make sense without the rest of the video? Is the quote accurate, or does it cut a sentence in half? Is the speaker's face in frame, and are the captions readable? Pick the best two or three and throw the rest away. A clip that needs explaining is not a clip.

One warning about cost: OpusClip charges by the minute of source video you upload, not by the clip. A 60-minute recording costs 60 credits whether it produces five clips or twenty. Do not upload a two-hour recording to test the tool; upload a 15-minute section first.

Step 4: When to generate video with AI — and when not to

Tools such as Runway can turn a written description into a few seconds of video, or animate a still image. The results can be striking. They are also expensive per second, unreliable for anything that must be accurate, and easy to misuse.

Use generated video for a supporting shot: a background texture, a simple illustration in motion, or a scene that is hard to film. Do not use it for anything a viewer would take as real footage — a place, a person, an event, a product. A generated clip of a person doing something they never did is not a creative choice; it is a misleading video, and platforms treat it that way.

The cost is the other reason to be careful. Runway charges by the second: its main model, Gen-4.5, costs 12 credits a second, so a 5-second clip costs 60 credits. The free plan's 125 one-time credits buy about ten seconds of Gen-4.5 — enough to test the quality, not to make videos. The cheaper Gen-4 Turbo is listed at 5 credits a second in Runway's help center and API docs, but Runway's own plan cards imply about 6 credits a second, so do not budget on the Turbo rate until you see it in your own account.

The label rule, in plain English

All three platforms require a label when AI creates or meaningfully changes something realistic — a person, a place, an event, or a voice a viewer could mistake for real. On YouTube, you answer the "altered or synthetic content" question when you upload, and since May 2026 YouTube may also add the label itself. TikTok requires its label on realistic-looking AI scenes or people. Meta's rule covers photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio, including a Reel narrated with a realistic AI-generated voiceover.

What does not need a label: an AI-written script, captions, color grading, a cloned voice of your own, or clearly cartoon content. The test is realism, not whether you used AI at all. When in doubt, turn the label on.

There is a second rule worth knowing before you invest months in this. YouTube's monetization policies target "inauthentic" content — mass-produced, templated videos with no original insight, commentary, or value added. AI-assisted content is allowed; AI as the entire creative process, with nothing of yours in it, is not reliably monetizable. TikTok likewise keeps unoriginal or reused material without anything new added out of the For You feed.

What it costs, and what you actually need to start

You can start for $0. A phone camera, the free version of one editor, and the platforms' own music libraries are enough for your first month. US prices below were checked in November 2026; prices vary by country and device, so check the vendor's page before you pay.

ToolFree planPaid plan, as checked
CapCut$0 — basic editing, auto-captions, 1080p exportPro $19.99/month or $179.99/year, 1,200 AI credits a month, 1 TB storage, 4K export
Descript$0 — 60 media minutes a month, 100 AI credits one-time, 720p with watermarkHobbyist $24/month or $16/month billed yearly (10 media hours); Creator $35/month or $24/month billed yearly (30 media hours, 4K)
OpusClip$0 — 60 credits a month, watermark, clips exportable for 3 days onlyStarter $15/month (150 credits, monthly billing only); Pro $29/month or $14.50/month billed yearly (300 credits)
Runway$0 — 125 credits one-time, watermarkedStandard $15/month or $12/month billed yearly (625 credits); Pro $35/month or $28/month billed yearly (2,250 credits)

Two details that catch people out. First, CapCut also sells a Standard plan at $9.99 a month in the US App Store — it is not listed on capcut.com's US pricing page, and its AI allowances are not published there. Second, credits are a real budget: CapCut Pro's 1,200 credits, Descript's media minutes, and OpusClip's source minutes all run out. OpusClip's paid credits roll over for up to two months, and its yearly Pro credits arrive as a lump sum. One editor is enough. If a tool costs $20 a month and you have not earned anything from the work it supports, pause it.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Editing before you have a script. A video with no clear point cannot be fixed in the edit. Write the one sentence the video promises, then record.
  • Trusting auto-captions without reading them. Names, numbers, and prices are where they fail first.
  • Generating video when recording is easier. A real 10-second clip of your product beats a generated one that took an hour and ten takes.
  • Uploading a two-hour video to a clipping tool on the free plan. You will spend the whole month's credits on one test.
  • Posting without the AI label when the video needs one. If a viewer could mistake AI video for real footage, turn the label on.

Conclusion

AI video tools are at their best on the slow, mechanical jobs: cutting pauses, adding captions, and finding the clips inside a long recording. You still choose the topic, write the script, record the video, check the captions, and decide whether a clip is honest enough to publish.

Start with one editor and one kind of video, post three useful clips a week for two months, and judge the work by whether people finish the video and come back.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Email JoJo's Blocks

Frequently asked questions

Which AI video tool should a beginner start with?⌄

The one that matches how you record. CapCut if you film on your phone and post short-form video; Descript if you talk to camera and the words matter most. Add a clipping tool only when you already have long videos to cut from.

Do I need the paid version of CapCut or Descript to start?⌄

No. Both have free plans that cover basic editing and captions. Only pay when you can name the limit you keep hitting — the number of media minutes, the export quality, or the AI credits.

Can AI captions be trusted?⌄

For a rough first draft, yes. For publishing, no — read every caption while watching the video, and check names, numbers, and prices first.

Do I need to label AI content in my videos?⌄

Yes, when it is realistic. If AI creates or changes a person, place, event, or realistic voice a viewer could mistake for real, turn on the platform's AI label. Scripts, captions, and cartoon-style content do not need one.

AI Note-Taking and Meeting Summaries: A Practical Beginner's Guide

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · note-taking, meetings

Picture the meeting after the meeting. One person is sure the launch moved to Friday. Another is sure it stayed on Tuesday. A third remembers someone promising to send the contract, but nobody remembers who. Everyone left the same call with a different memory of it.

An AI note-taker fixes that specific problem. It records the call, writes a transcript, and produces a short summary with the decisions and action items, so the record no longer depends on whoever scribbled fastest. Used well, it saves the hour you would have spent retyping notes. Used badly, it records people who never agreed to be recorded, or hands you a summary with the wrong date.

This guide covers choosing the right tool, a simple before-during-after routine, and checking the result before anyone relies on it — plus the one thing beginners most often skip: asking permission.

What an AI note-taker actually does

A meeting note-taker joins a video call — usually as a small bot in the participant list — records the audio, turns it into a transcript, and uses AI to write a summary: the main points, the decisions, and who promised to do what by when. Most tools also let you search old meetings and ask questions about them.

That is different from a notes app like Notion AI, which captures your own thoughts: you type or dictate, and the AI turns it into a summary, a list, or a first draft. This guide covers both, starting with meetings, where the stakes are higher.

Two honest limits. First, no transcription is perfect: names, numbers, dates, and accents are where errors cluster. Second, a summary is not a record of what was said — it is the AI's interpretation of it. Treat it as a draft you check, not a minute you can quote.

Step 1: Choose the right tool for the way you meet

Pick one that matches where your meetings already happen. Start with the tool you already pay for: on Google Workspace Business Standard or above, Gemini is already there. Otherwise, try one free plan for a month and judge it on real meetings before paying.

ToolBest forFree planPaid plan, as checked
Otter.aiOne person, short calls on Zoom, Meet, or Teams$0 — 300 minutes a month, 30 minutes per conversation, 3 lifetime file importsPro $16.99/month or $8.33/month billed yearly (1,200 min, 90-min calls); Business $30/month or $19.99/month billed yearly (unlimited, 4-hour calls)
Fireflies.aiClient calls you want to keep and search$0 — 400 minutes of storage per team; new accounts get 3 transcribed meetings unless auto-join is onPro $10/seat/month billed yearly or $18 monthly (8,000 min storage); Business $19 billed yearly or $29 monthly (unlimited storage, 3-hour meetings)
Gemini in Google MeetGoogle Workspace users — no bot, no second appNo free plan; from Business Standard, $14/user/month billed yearlyBusiness Plus $22/user/month; Google AI Pro $19.99/month (meetings you host)
Notion AINotes you write yourself, inside NotionTrial only on Free and PlusFull AI with Business, $20/member/month billed yearly ($24 monthly)

A few details that decide the choice. Fireflies transcribes in 100+ languages and adds video recording and downloads on paid plans; recordings stop at 2 hours on Free and Pro, and at 3 hours on Business. Gemini's notes are switched on by the organizer, whose plan decides whether the feature exists in a given call — not yours. They work in eight languages, one per meeting. Notion's standalone AI add-on was retired in May 2025, and its AI Meeting Notes work without a bot joining the call.

Step 2: A simple routine — before, during, and after the meeting

This routine takes five minutes around a meeting and prevents most of the common mistakes.

Before: ask permission and set the agenda. Tell everyone, in the invite or at the start, that an AI note-taker will record and summarize the meeting, and what will happen to the notes. If anyone objects, turn it off. Then write a short agenda: the decision you need, in one sentence, and the two or three questions the meeting must answer.

During: take two lines of your own notes. Do not stop listening because the bot is recording. Write down the two things that matter most: the decision and the deadline. If the conversation turns confidential — salaries, discipline, a client's private details — pause the recording.

After: check the summary before you share it. Read it the same day and check four things: the decisions, the dates, the names, and who was assigned what. Fix errors in the document itself — the shared copy is the one people will quote. Then send it to everyone who was there, with the action items at the top and the transcript linked below.

Step 3: Check the accuracy — names, numbers, and dates first

AI transcription is usually good enough to follow a conversation — and that is what makes its errors dangerous: a fluent summary with one wrong number looks trustworthy. Check in this order.

Names. The tool may mishear a name or give a quote to the wrong speaker, especially when two people talk at once. If the summary says "Sarah will send the contract" and it was Sara, the wrong person gets chased.

Numbers and dates. Prices, budgets, and deadlines are where errors cluster. A summary that says "$5,000" when the meeting agreed "$15,000" is worse than no summary at all. Read every number and date against your own notes, and against the transcript if they disagree.

Decisions versus discussion. AI summaries sometimes present something merely discussed as something decided. "We talked about moving the launch" is not "we decided to move the launch." If the summary claims a decision, check the transcript for the words "let's do that" or "agreed" before you tell anyone else.

Quotes. Never quote a person from an AI summary. If a quote matters — a client promising something, a manager approving a budget — check the transcript, and ideally the recording, before you put their words in an email.

For the first month, spend two minutes after every meeting comparing the summary with the transcript. You will quickly see your tool's pattern: the names it always gets wrong, the accents it struggles with, the numbers it drops.

Step 4: Consent and privacy — the part beginners skip

An AI note-taker is a recording device, and recording people without their agreement is where beginners get into real trouble. Three rules:

Announce it, every time. Say at the start that a note-taker is recording, and name the tool. Most tools show a bot in the participant list — a notice, but not consent, and on a busy call nobody may notice it. A sentence at the start is the reliable version. If someone asks you to stop, stop.

Know the law where your participants are. In the United States, federal law and most states require only one party's consent — but about a dozen states, including California, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Washington, require every participant's consent, and a call crossing state lines should follow the strictest state involved. In the EU, UK, Canada, and Australia, businesses also need a lawful reason and clear notice. This is general information, not legal advice — but the safe practice is the same everywhere: announce, get agreement, stop if anyone objects.

Know where the recording goes. A transcript lives on someone else's servers. Before a sensitive meeting, check the privacy terms: does the tool use recordings to train its AI, who can read the transcript, how long is it kept? Otter's privacy policy (effective June 2026) allows training on de-identified recordings and transcripts, and a US class action over recording without consent is pending — in August 2026 a federal judge let the core claims proceed to discovery, with no ruling yet that Otter broke the law. Fireflies faces a separate pending case in Illinois over voice recordings. Google says Workspace content is not used to train its models outside the customer's domain without permission. Read the terms before the first sensitive meeting, not after it, and never record a meeting about someone's health, salary, or performance without a clear reason and their agreement.

What it costs, and when paying is worth it

You can start for $0 — every tool above has a free plan, or a feature included in a plan you may already have — and a free plan is enough for a month of real meetings. US prices were checked in November 2026, before tax; check the vendor's pricing page before you pay.

Pay only when you can name the limit you keep hitting: meetings longer than 30 minutes, a storage cap that fills up, or summaries you actually use every week. Do not pay for two note-takers at once — one tool, used for a month, teaches you what you need.

Solo notes: when there is no meeting at all

Not every note needs a recording. Working alone, write a rough note, then ask the AI to turn it into a summary, a checklist, or a first draft — Notion AI is built for this, and ChatGPT or Claude can do it from a pasted note. The AI can organize your thinking, but it cannot know what you meant, so read the summary back. And do not paste passwords, bank details, or a client's private information into an AI tool.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Recording without telling anyone. A bot in the participant list is not consent. Announce it, and stop if someone objects.
  • Sending the summary without reading it. One wrong date sent to a client costs more trust than the summary saved.
  • Quoting people from a summary. Check the transcript first — summaries invent confident wording that nobody actually said.
  • Keeping transcripts you do not need. Delete them when the work is done, especially for sensitive meetings.
  • Paying for two note-takers. One tool, used for a month, tells you what you actually need.
  • Pasting private information into an AI note tool. Passwords, bank details, and a client's confidential information do not belong in a prompt.

Conclusion

AI note-taking is at its best on the slow, mechanical jobs: capturing what was said, turning it into a short summary, and pulling out the decisions and deadlines. It saves time by removing the retyping, not the thinking. You still set the agenda, ask permission, listen, and check the summary before anyone acts on it.

Start with one tool and one habit: announce the recording, check the decisions, dates, and names, and send the checked summary the same day.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to tell people an AI note-taker is recording?⌄

Yes — announce it at the start of every meeting and name the tool. In several US states and in the EU, UK, Canada, and Australia, recording without agreement can break the law.

Which AI note-taker should a beginner start with?⌄

The one that matches where you already meet: Gemini on Google Workspace Business Standard or above; Otter for a simple free start across Zoom, Meet, and Teams; Fireflies to keep and search recordings. Try one free plan for a month before paying.

How accurate are AI meeting summaries?⌄

Good enough to follow a conversation, not good enough to trust blindly. Names, numbers, dates, and who said what are the most common errors — check those four things before you share a summary, and never quote a person from a summary without checking the transcript.

What happens to my meeting recordings?⌄

It depends on the tool: recordings and transcripts sit on the vendor's servers, and some vendors use de-identified recordings to train their AI. Read the privacy terms before the first sensitive meeting, and delete transcripts you no longer need.

Using AI for Spreadsheets: Formulas, Data Cleanup and Simple Analysis

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · spreadsheets, ai-tools

Somewhere in your business there is a spreadsheet with a wrong total in it. A total that is $150 out, or a month's sales counted twice, or a product that quietly vanished from a sum because its name was spelled differently. Nobody noticed, because the number looked confident.

That is the whole problem with AI in spreadsheets, and the whole point of this guide. AI is genuinely good at the language-shaped jobs — writing a formula, tidying a messy column, turning a question into a chart. It is a bad fit for one thing: the final number. A language model predicts words, not numbers, and a wrong total that looks confident is worse than no total at all.

The rule for this guide is simple: ask the AI to build the calculator, then check the calculator.

The four ways AI gets into your spreadsheet

You do not need a new app — AI reaches spreadsheets through four routes, and you probably already have one.

1. Built into Google Sheets — Gemini. On Workspace Business Standard ($14 per user a month, annual billing) or Business Plus ($22), Gemini is built into Sheets: a side panel that builds tables, writes formulas, makes charts and pivot tables, and answers questions about your data. A personal account needs Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month); Business Starter ($7) excludes Gemini in Sheets. Sheets also has the =AI() function, which runs a prompt inside a cell — categorize a row, summarize a note — one row at a time.

2. Built into Excel — Copilot. Microsoft 365 Personal ($9.99 a month or $99.99 a year) and Family ($12.99 a month or $129.99 a year) include Copilot in Excel through AI credits, for the subscription owner only. Premium ($19.99 a month or $199.99 a year) gives extensive usage. Business plans add Copilot separately — check Microsoft's current business pricing before you budget on it. Copilot works as a side panel: it answers questions, writes formulas, builds charts, and in its editing modes changes cells directly. It needs AutoSave on, so the file must live in OneDrive.

3. A chat assistant — ChatGPT or Claude. Both let you upload a spreadsheet and talk about it. ChatGPT takes XLSX, XLS, CSV, and TSV files of about 50 MB, with roughly 3 uploads a day on the free plan. Claude takes files up to 500 MB each and 20 per chat, though XLSX needs code execution switched on. Both write formulas to paste in, explain a formula you inherited, and build a fresh spreadsheet from a description. Both also have Excel add-ins: ChatGPT for Excel works from the free plan up (limited on Free and Go), Claude for Excel from Claude Pro ($20 a month, or $17 billed yearly).

4. A newer option — Claude Sheets. Anthropic launched Claude Sheets in beta on 10 November 2026, on paid Claude plans only. The AI writes real formulas rather than guessing totals, with grids capped at 100,000 cells and 144 functions at launch — but no pivot tables yet, no macros, and no live data from your other apps. It is promising and unproven, not somewhere to move your accounts yet.

Start with the tool you already pay for. If you live in Google Sheets, that is Gemini; in Excel, Copilot or one of the add-ins. Paying for a second only makes sense once you can name a job the first keeps failing at.

Worked example: the formula that pays for itself

Say you run a small shop and have a sheet of orders: column A is the date, column B is the product, column C is the quantity, column D is the price. You want total revenue for each product in November. Instead of hunting for the right function, ask the AI in plain words:

"My sheet has dates in column A, products in column B, quantities in column C and prices in column D. Write a formula for total revenue for 'mug' in November 2026."

A good answer is a formula with a sentence explaining each part — something like a SUMIFS that multiplies quantity by price only where the product is "mug" and the date falls in November. Paste it in, then check it like a colleague's work: change one value and watch the total move, compare it against a sample you counted by hand, and read it to see it references the right columns.

Three habits make this reliable. First, describe the layout exactly: column letters, what is in each one, and the exceptions (blank rows, a header row, dates stored as text). Second, ask for the formula, not the answer — it keeps the math inside the spreadsheet, where it can be re-checked. Third, ask it to explain a formula you do not understand: paste in one you inherited and ask it to walk through it.

What not to do: do not paste a formula in and trust it because the AI sounded sure. A SUMIFS that quietly excludes a whole category runs without an error message.

Step 2: Clean up messy data before you analyze it

Real data is messy: "mug" and "Mug" and "MUG" in one column, a date typed three different ways, an empty cell where a price should be. AI is good at this tidy-up because it is a language job, not a math job — but the same rule applies: check the result.

Standardize text. Ask the AI for a formula that turns a column into consistent case. In Sheets, the =AI() function can categorize a column — "label each customer reply as praise, complaint, or question" — row by row.

Fix dates and numbers. Ask the AI for a formula that converts "Nov 5" and "05/11/2026" into the same date, or flags rows where a price is stored as text. Then sort the column: errors cluster at the top and bottom.

Find the duplicates and the gaps. Ask the AI to help you find duplicate orders or missing values, then decide yourself what to do with them — deleting a duplicate is a business decision, not a formula's job.

One caution: never paste sensitive data into a chat assistant without thinking about where it goes. Customer names, email addresses, bank details, and salary figures do not belong in a prompt. If the data is private, use the AI built into your own spreadsheet, where the file stays in your account. And work on a copy, so a mistake is undoable.

A note on the =AI() cell limit, because Google's own pages disagree — and the disagreement has a real explanation. The Help Center page for the AI function says only the first 350 selected cells generate per run. Google's Workspace update of 28 October 2026 says Fill with Gemini, the bulk-fill entry point that runs on the same function, supports up to 3,000 cells per request. In practice: try a small sample first, fill in batches, and do not plan a 2,000-row job around either number until you have seen it work on your account.

Step 3: Ask questions about your data — and check every answer

Once the data is clean, ask the AI questions in plain words: "Which product earned the most in October?", "How many orders came from each city?", "Show me a chart of weekly sales." Gemini and Copilot both do this, building the chart or pivot table for you.

This is where the honesty matters most. Independent benchmarks are sobering, and they need reading carefully. On SpreadsheetBench, 912 real-world tasks taken from Excel forums, Gemini in Sheets scored 70.48% in March 2026 — the highest of the four major assistants, as self-reported by Google, though tuned agent systems have since posted higher scores on the same leaderboard. On the harder follow-up, SpreadsheetBench 2, built from 321 end-to-end business workflows, the best plain model completed only 34.89% of tasks (Claude Opus 4.6, June 2026), with tuned agent systems reaching about 55%. Different tests, different setups — do not average them.

So run every AI answer through three checks:

1. The reference total. Before you ask, know one number by hand — total revenue for the month, the number of orders, the biggest single sale. If the AI's answer disagrees with a number you trust, the AI is wrong, not your records.

2. The spot check. Pick three rows the answer depends on and verify them by hand. If it says the top product is mugs, check the mug rows yourself.

3. The sanity check. Does the answer make sense? A chart saying December outsold November tenfold is a signal to stop and look, not to copy the number into an email.

If a number will go into a quote, an invoice, a tax return, or a money decision, check it twice — against the raw data and a formula you can see.

What it costs, and what you actually need

You can start for $0: Google Sheets and Excel on the web are free, and ChatGPT's free plan takes spreadsheet uploads and includes the Excel add-in with limited usage. Prices below were checked in November 2026.

ToolFree way inPaid, as checked
Gemini in SheetsNot on a free account or StarterBusiness Standard $14/user/month; Google AI Pro $19.99/month
Copilot in ExcelNot on a free accountPersonal $9.99/month (owner only); Premium $19.99/month; business add-on — check Microsoft's current business pricing
ChatGPT for ExcelFree plan, limitedGo $8; Plus $20; Pro from $100/month
Claude for ExcelNo free planPro $20/month ($17 yearly); Max from $100/month

Pay only when you can name the limit you keep hitting: uploads, AI credits, or needing the AI inside the workbook daily. One spreadsheet AI is enough to start.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Asking for the final number. Ask for the formula. A formula can be checked; a number in a chat reply cannot.
  • Trusting a confident-sounding answer. AI tools do not express uncertainty when they are wrong. Your checks are the uncertainty.
  • Letting the AI delete or overwrite data. Work on a copy, and keep the original.
  • Pasting private data into a chat. Customer details, bank numbers, and salaries stay out of prompts.
  • Analyzing before cleaning, or using an AI total for money decisions without a second check. A quote deserves a formula you can see and a total you can reproduce.

Conclusion

AI in spreadsheets is at its best on the slow, language-shaped jobs: writing a formula you can paste in and test, tidying a messy column, turning a question into a chart. You still describe the layout, read the formula, and check the total against a number you trust.

Start with one job and one tool you already have: pick a formula you keep looking up, ask the AI to write it, test it on five rows, and check the total by hand.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Frequently asked questions

Which AI should a beginner start with for spreadsheets?⌄

The one built into the spreadsheet you already use — Gemini in Sheets, Copilot or an add-in in Excel. Add a chat assistant only when the built-in tool cannot reach a file.

Can I trust AI to add up my numbers?⌄

Not blindly. Benchmarks show success rates well below 100%, and wrong totals are often only slightly wrong. Ask for the formula, put it in the sheet, and check the total against a number you know.

Do I need to pay for AI in spreadsheets?⌄

No. Google Sheets and Excel on the web are free, and ChatGPT's free plan handles spreadsheet uploads and the Excel add-in with limited usage. Pay when you hit a limit you can name — uploads, AI credits, or needing the AI inside the workbook daily. And keep private data out of chat prompts: built-in AI keeps the file inside your account, while a chat assistant sends a copy to the vendor.

articles.excerpt: A citation is not proof. Learn a five-step AI research routine: ask a checkable question, spot the classic errors, and verify the claims that matter.
articles.bodyHtml:

AI Tools & Online Business

An AI Research Workflow That Checks Its Sources

By JoJo's Blocks · 2026-11-18 · 10 min read · ai-research, fact-checking

Ask an AI assistant a research question and you will get an answer in seconds — confident, well written, and full of citations. That speed is real, and so is the problem underneath it: a citation is not proof. The link may open, the page may exist, and the sentence beside it may still say something the page never said.

That is not a reason to stop using AI for research. Use it the way a careful researcher would: let the AI do the slow work of finding and sorting material, then check the claims that matter yourself, against the original source, before you trust, quote, or publish them.

What AI research tools actually do

There are two kinds of AI research, and beginners often confuse them.

The first is web research: you ask a question, the tool searches the web, reads some pages, and writes an answer with links. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity all do this, and their "deep research" modes do it more thoroughly — they plan a search, run several rounds, and produce a longer report, usually in five to thirty minutes.

The second is research inside your own files: you upload documents — PDFs, articles, your own notes — and ask questions about them. Google's NotebookLM, renamed Gemini Notebook in July 2026, works this way. It answers only from the material you gave it, and points to the exact passage each claim comes from. It cannot invent a source that was never in your pile, though it can still misread one.

Neither kind replaces reading.

Step 1: Choose the right tool for the question

Start with the tool you already pay for.

ToolBest forFree planPaid plan, as checked
ChatGPTEveryday questions, plus deep research reports$0 — web search and limited deep researchGo $8/month; Plus $20/month; Pro from $100/month
GeminiResearch inside Google's world — Gmail, Drive, Docs$0 — Deep Research included, standard limitsGoogle AI Plus $4.99/month; Pro $19.99/month; Ultra $99.99 or $199.99/month
PerplexityQuick answers with sources shown up front$0 — basic searches, 3 Pro Searches a day, 1 Research query a monthPro $20/month or $17/month billed yearly ($200/year); Max $200/month or $167/month billed yearly
ClaudeLong documents and careful, sourced writing$0 — web search included, but no Research modePro $20/month ($17 billed yearly); Max $100/month; Ultra $200/month
NotebookLM / Gemini NotebookQuestions about your own documents$0 — 100 notebooks, 50 sources per notebookVia Google AI plans: Plus $4.99/month; Pro $19.99/month

Two details to know: OpenAI no longer publishes a fixed per-plan deep research count, so the "25 a month" figure in older guides is out of date, and since May 2026 Gemini's personal plans use a compute-based limit, not a fixed number of reports. Claude's Research mode runs only on paid plans and draws on the same usage pool as your chats. NotebookLM has no standalone subscription: the higher limits come bundled inside Google AI plans, with Plus at 200 notebooks and 100 sources each, and Pro at 500 notebooks and 300 sources each.

Step 2: Ask a question the tool can actually answer

A vague question gets a vague answer, and a vague answer is hard to check. Before you ask, write the question down in one sentence, and add three things that make it checkable.

The decision it serves. "What is the best email tool?" has no answer. "Which email tool under $30 a month lets a beginner send a weekly newsletter to under 1,000 subscribers?" can be answered and checked.

The facts you need, named. Prices, dates, limits, names.

What counts as a good source. Ask for primary sources where they exist: the vendor's own pricing page, the official help center, the regulator's own site. Add this to your prompt: "Answer with citations. Prefer primary sources. If a fact comes only from a secondary source, say so. If you cannot verify a fact, say that instead of guessing."

That last instruction matters most: AI models would rather guess than say they do not know.

A worked trace: follow one claim to its source

Here is the routine in action, on a claim you might actually meet: "Perplexity Pro costs $17 a month."

  1. Read the answer, then open the link. The AI cites Perplexity's Pro page. Open it yourself. It says $17 a month billed annually. That is a real number — on that page.
  2. Open a second source. Perplexity's pricing hub lists Pro at $20 a month. Both pages are official, and both are current. The difference is the billing basis: $20 is the monthly rate, $17 is the monthly equivalent of a $200 yearly bill.
  3. Write down what you actually know. "Pro is $20 a month, or $200 a year — $17 a month equivalent."

Step 3: Read the answer like a skeptic, not a fan

When the answer arrives, read it for the claims you would repeat to someone else — those are the ones that need checking.

Separate facts from framing. "This tool is popular" is framing. "This tool costs $20 a month" is a fact. Circle the facts: prices, dates, numbers, names, and anything you would put in a blog post or a decision about money.

Check the date of every source. A pricing page from 2024 is not evidence about a price in 2026.

Watch for the three classic errors. First, a real link attached to a claim the page does not support — the most common failure in independent tests. Second, a plausible-sounding study, quote, or statistic that does not exist at all. Third, a number that is close but wrong — a price from the wrong plan, a figure from the wrong region, a date from the wrong year. Close-but-wrong is the hardest kind to catch.

Do not trust confidence or length. A long, detailed report with many citations can still be wrong. The studies below disagree with each other on the exact rate, because they tested different tools on different tasks — do not average them.

What the studies actually found — kept separate

Each study below used a different method and tested different things. Read them as separate warnings, not as one combined score.

  • Liu, Zhang, and Liang (2023): in an audit of four generative search engines, only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations.
  • Tow Center, Columbia (March 2025): eight AI search tools were given excerpts from real news articles and asked to identify the source. Collectively they got more than 60% of the 1,600 queries wrong. ChatGPT Search was wrong on 134 of 200 and declined to answer none of them; Perplexity did best at 37% wrong, Grok 3 worst at 94%.
  • Walters and Wilder (2023): in 84 short literature reviews written by ChatGPT, 55% of GPT-3.5's references and 18% of GPT-4's references were fabricated outright.
  • DeepTRACE, Salesforce (September 2025): citation accuracy of 40–80% across deep-research systems.
  • EBU/BBC (October 2025): 45% of AI answers about news had a significant issue, and 31% had serious sourcing problems.
  • Onweller and colleagues, Cited but Not Verified (May 2026): factual accuracy of 39–77% across 14 models, even though more than 94% of the links worked.

Step 4: Check the three claims that matter most

You do not need to verify every sentence — just the three kinds of claim that cause real damage when they are wrong.

1. Anything involving money. Prices, fees, limits, refunds. Open the vendor's own pricing page yourself and find the number. Prices change often — Perplexity's Pro price has been listed at both $17 a month billed yearly and $20 a month billed monthly, as the worked trace above shows — so check the page on the day you need the figure.

2. Anything you will quote or publish. A statistic, a study, a quote, a legal rule. Open the source and read the sentence the AI is relying on. If the page does not contain it, the claim is unverified, however confident the answer sounded. If the claim is a study, check that it exists: search for its title, its authors, and its DOI, and confirm the DOI belongs to that study in a registry such as Crossref. A DOI that belongs to a different paper is a clear sign the reference was invented.

3. Anything that changes a decision. If the answer would make you buy a tool, cancel a service, or tell a client something, check it against a second, independent source. One source is a lead. Two sources that agree — ideally one of them primary — is a finding. If two good sources disagree, say so in your notes.

Step 5: Keep your sources, so you can prove what you found

Research you cannot retrace is research you cannot defend. Keep a short source list for anything you will use again: the question you asked, the tool and date, and the three or four primary sources you actually opened, with the date you opened them. A link is not enough — pages change. Copy the sentence or number you relied on into your notes, with the page name and date. Keep the files themselves if you use NotebookLM, so its answers can still point back to the passages they came from.

What it costs, and when paying is worth it

You can do serious research for $0: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity all offer web search and some deep research free, Claude offers web search free, and NotebookLM is free with a Google account. US prices were checked in November 2026, before tax; check the vendor's pricing page before you pay.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Quoting a citation you never opened. A link that works is not a claim that is true.
  • Trusting a report because it is long. Length is not evidence.
  • Accepting a study, quote, or statistic without checking it exists. Search for the title, the authors, and the DOI before you repeat it.
  • Using an old source for a current fact. Prices, plans, and limits change. Check the date on the page.
  • Asking one tool and stopping. If a claim would change a decision, check it against a second, independent source.
  • Pasting private information into a research tool. Customer details, bank numbers, and confidential documents do not belong in a prompt.

Conclusion

AI research tools are at their best on the slow, mechanical jobs: searching widely, reading quickly, and sorting what they found into a shape you can work with. You still write the question, decide which claims matter, open the sources, and check the facts before anyone else relies on them.

JoJo's Blocks — a note, and how to reach us

If you would like help learning to use AI tools, choosing the right AI software, or building a simple AI-assisted workflow for content creation and everyday business tasks, JoJo's Blocks offers personal AI learning and consulting.

And if you run a business, brand, or product and would like to reach a Pinterest audience, we also offer paid Pinterest promotion and partnership opportunities — with no promise of specific views, clicks, sales, or results.

Frequently asked questions

Which AI research tool should a beginner start with?⌄

The one you already have. ChatGPT or Gemini for web questions, Perplexity if you want sources shown up front, Claude for long documents, and NotebookLM for your own files. Try one free plan for a month before paying.

Can I trust AI citations?⌄

Not blindly. Independent studies have found that a large share of AI citations do not fully support the sentence beside them, and some references are invented entirely. Treat every citation as a lead: open the page and read the sentence.

What is the difference between web search and deep research?⌄

Web search answers a question in seconds from a few pages. Deep research plans a search, runs several rounds of it, and produces a longer cited report, usually in five to thirty minutes. Use it for questions with several parts, not for a single fact.

How do I check whether a study an AI cited is real?⌄

Search for its title and authors, and check its DOI in a registry such as Crossref. The DOI must exist and belong to the study named. If you cannot find it, do not quote it.
